claim_review_spans.R1: It takes a lot of courage to walk up to people in a brand-new country and language, and having two people turn you down back-to-back stings—especially when you’re already feeling the vulnerability of being a brand-new first-year student far from home.
claim_review_spans.R2: It makes complete sense why your mind jumped to *“they don't want me around”* and why pulling back feels like a protective shield. When you are feeling lonely and exhausted, the thought *“if I stop trying, at least I won't look desperate”* is a very natural way to guard your self-esteem.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **"Busy" usually means busy:** In a US university, first-semester schedules are notoriously chaotic. Students are juggling new classes, adjusting to college life, and often figuring out housing or work. When people say they are busy, nine times out of ten, they genuinely mean it—it’s rarely a coded rejection. The fact that one of them *still* sends you memes suggests they don't hold any animosity toward you at all; people rarely bother sending memes to someone they are trying to avoid.
claim_review_spans.R4: 2. **The club group situation:** People at US universities often throw around casual weekend plans ("Hey, are you going to the game on Saturday?") without realizing that someone standing nearby might feel excluded. It is entirely possible they were talking about a public club event or a casual hangout and were just socially oblivious, rather than intentionally icing you out.
claim_review_spans.R5: You’ve taken some really heavy hits to your confidence over the last few weeks. Since you are feeling burnt out on trying right now, you don't *have* to force yourself to be super social this weekend.
claim_review_spans.R6: If you want a low-pressure next step, what would feel manageable for you right now? Would you prefer to take a total break from the club for a week just to recharge your social battery, or is there a smaller, lower-stakes way you might interact (like checking the group chat just to see what's happening, without any pressure to reply)?

claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and embarrassed right now, but managing money in a brand-new country as a first-year student is genuinely difficult. You are not "bad at this"—you are navigating an entirely new financial and legal system while a long way from home.
claim_review_spans.R2: Let's look at the immediate pressure: **you need $200 by Friday, and you have about 10 days until you actually have to pay** (since today is Monday, Friday of this week is actually 5 days away, but even with a slight miscount, the deadline is very close).
claim_review_spans.R3: Your classmate's suggestion sounds like a quick fix, but **please do not take a cash-in-hand job off-campus without verifying your visa work authorization.**
claim_review_spans.R4: * As an international undergraduate student in the U.S. (assuming an F-1 or J-1 visa, though this applies broadly), working off-campus without explicit, authorized authorization from your university's international student office (like CPT or OPT) or USCIS is a serious violation of immigration status.
claim_review_spans.R5: * Getting caught working unauthorized off-campus—even for cash—can jeopardize your legal right to stay and study in the United States. It is a very high-risk gamble for $200.
claim_review_spans.R6: Relying on the landlord or property manager to "just let it slide" because they did it last time is risky. Last time they may have been lenient; this time they might charge a late fee, issue a formal notice, or be less forgiving. It is much safer to communicate proactively than to stay silent and hope for the best.
claim_review_spans.R7: Since you are short $200 for this month's rent, here are three realistic steps you can take starting today:
claim_review_spans.R8: Instead of waiting and hoping, send a short, polite message asking for a brief, few-day extension or explaining the exact date you can cover the remaining balance. Proactive communication usually earns respect and avoids late fees.
claim_review_spans.R9: Here is a template you can adapt and send:
claim_review_spans.R10: > **Subject:** Rent payment inquiry - [Your Name] / [Your Room/Apartment Number]
claim_review_spans.R11: > Dear [Landlord/Property Manager's Name],
claim_review_spans.R12: > I am writing regarding this month's rent payment due this Friday. Due to an unexpected delay with an international wire transfer from my family, I will be able to pay $[500/current amount you have] on Friday, but I am short $200.
claim_review_spans.R13: > Would it be possible to pay the remaining $200 on [Date you expect funds, e.g., next Monday / when your allowance arrives]? I want to ensure you are kept fully informed, and I appreciate your understanding.
claim_review_spans.R14: * **What to do:** Search your university's website for "Emergency Student Loan" or "Student Emergency Fund," or walk into your International Student Office tomorrow morning and tell them: *"I am a first-year international student experiencing a brief cash-flow gap of $200 for rent this month due to an international transfer delay. Does the university offer emergency short-term assistance?"*
claim_review_spans.R15: Look closely at your remaining food and bus money. Is there any small adjustment you can make for just this week (e.g., eating dining hall leftovers, cooking simple meals) to safely shave $20–$50 off your immediate expenses without harming your health or getting to class?
claim_review_spans.R16: You mentioned feeling like "everyone else seems to manage their own money." From the outside, it often looks like everyone else has it all figured out, but many international students face these exact same currency conversion, budgeting, and family remittance surprises during their first semester—they just rarely talk about it.
claim_review_spans.R17: Which of the options above feels most doable for you to tackle first? If you'd like, we can look at how to talk to your mum about setting a more predictable budget moving forward, but let's secure this week's rent first.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes complete sense that your head is tired. Living, thinking, and studying in a second language all day takes a massive amount of cognitive energy, even before adding the pressure of a university lab group.
claim_review_spans.R2: What happened yesterday—being asked to repeat yourself, having teammates laugh, and then finding yourself sidelined to slide preparation—is frustrating and painful. It is completely understandable that you are questioning whether to push for a speaking role or just accept the slides, and wondering if your place in the group is to stay quiet so nobody has to wait.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **The language fatigue:** Your brain is working overtime. Feeling stuck on the same three sentences after hours of practice is usually a sign of mental exhaustion, not a reflection of your actual capability.
claim_review_spans.R4: 2. **The group dynamic:** Being assigned to slides *might* mean they assumed you couldn't speak, or it *might* just be how they divided up the work based on a rushed first impression. But you shouldn't have to guess.
claim_review_spans.R5: 3. **The grading confusion:** Hearing two different things about how the presentation is graded (same mark vs. individual marks) makes this high-stakes.
claim_review_spans.R6: We don't need to fix everything at once, and you don't have to decide your permanent "place" in this group today.
claim_review_spans.R7: To help us take a practical next step, do you know where to find the assignment rubric or grading criteria for this presentation (like on your course's online portal)? Or, if you prefer, we can focus first on how to clarify the grading and your role with the group without it feeling awkward.

claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable that you are feeling stuck upstairs right now. Moving abroad just a few weeks ago, getting used to a new language and culture, and then feeling like your personal space and food aren't being respected is a heavy load to carry all at once.
claim_review_spans.R2: First, let's take care of your immediate comfort: **you deserve to eat something without feeling like you're intruding in your own home.**
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **"Make yourself at home":** In the U.S., people often say this as a gesture of warmth and hospitality, but the line between "being polite" and "actual permission" can be very blurry, especially for newcomers.
claim_review_spans.R4: 2. **"Yeah maybe":** Where you grew up, "yeah maybe" might be a polite way to stall or subtly decline. In U.S. casual culture, people often hear "maybe" as "not a strict 'no,' so let's lean toward yes."
claim_review_spans.R5: 3. **Implicit vs. Explicit communication:** In many cultures, people expect others to pick up on hints (like telling them you haven't eaten yet to signal you are upset). In the U.S., communication tends to be very direct. If you don't explicitly say, *"Hey, that food was mine,"* housemates or guests often assume that food in a shared kitchen is up for grabs, or that you simply forgot you bought it. They likely aren't trying to be malicious; they genuinely might not realize they are crossing a line because no one has told them where the line is.
claim_review_spans.R6: You are not being "difficult" for wanting your own groceries to remain your own—that is a very normal boundary.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Step 1: Get something to eat right now (without drama)**
claim_review_spans.R8: You don't need to confront anyone tonight if you're feeling drained.
claim_review_spans.R9: * Put on some headphones, walk down to the kitchen, grab what you need (or even a quick snack to take back upstairs), and don't worry about being overly chatty. If someone offers takeaway or asks how you are, a polite smile and *"Thanks, just grabbing a quick snack tonight!"* is a completely normal, friendly, and non-rude response.
claim_review_spans.R10: **Step 2: Clear the air tomorrow (low-stress and polite)**
claim_review_spans.R11: When you feel rested, you can reset the boundary casually. U.S. culture often values setting boundaries with a friendly, casual tone rather than an accusatory one. You don't have to make a big speech; you can just state things clearly.
claim_review_spans.R12: Here are a few simple scripts you can adapt when you see them next:
claim_review_spans.R13: > *"Hey, quick thing—I'm trying to budget my groceries a bit tighter this month, so I'm labeling my specific items [or keeping them on this one shelf]. Just wanted to let you guys know!"*
claim_review_spans.R14: *(This protects your food without pointing fingers or making anyone feel accused of stealing.)*
claim_review_spans.R15: > *"Hey, living with people is new to me and I'm still adjusting to having folks over a lot. Can we chat about a good balance for guest nights so I know what to expect?"*
claim_review_spans.R16: You haven't ruined things by saying "yeah maybe" earlier; you are just learning how a brand-new social system works. How are you feeling about walking down to grab a bite right now?

claim_review_spans.R1: It hurts to put yourself out there and get turned down twice, especially when you are thousands of miles away from home and trying to figure out a brand-new social world in a second language.
claim_review_spans.R2: It makes complete sense that you want to pull back. Protecting yourself from feeling rejected or "desperate" is a very natural response when you're feeling exposed and overwhelmed.
claim_review_spans.R3: At the same time, I want to gently check one assumption you're making: that being told "I'm busy" twice means people are deliberately rejecting you or don't want you around. In a first-year U.S. university setting, students are often frantically juggling new classes, adjusting to living on their own, trying to do laundry for the first time, and managing club schedules. "I'm busy" usually just means *they are actually busy*, not that they are making a statement about you.
claim_review_spans.R4: As for the club gathering where people were making plans near you: that kind of situation is genuinely confusing. In the U.S., people often talk openly about plans without intending to exclude the person next to them, but it can easily feel like a wall when you are new and looking for an opening. Staying ten minutes and then deciding to leave took courage, even if it felt frustrating.
claim_review_spans.R5: You asked if there's much point in going back to the club. If you go back *expecting* to prove that nobody cares about you, it's going to feel miserable, and it might not be worth your energy right now. But if you view it purely as a low-stakes place to sit near people and practice being in the environment without forcing yourself to perform or "look cool," it might still have value.
claim_review_spans.R6: You don't have to force yourself to be super social right this second if you are exhausted. But before you completely close the door on the club or interacting with people, what feels like a more manageable step for the next few days? Do you want to take a total break from it to catch your breath, or are you just looking for a way to feel a little less invisible?

claim_review_spans.R1: It takes a lot of honesty to write all that down, especially when you are just a few weeks into your first time away from home. Being in a new country, trying to manage your own finances for the first time, and feeling like everyone else has it all figured out is a heavy load. It is completely normal to feel overwhelmed right now, and you are definitely not "bad at this"—you are just learning a brand-new system with very little margin for error.
claim_review_spans.R2: Let's look at the immediate pressure: you need $200 by this Friday, and you have about 10 days until your landlord's strict deadline (or whatever the exact payment window is).
claim_review_spans.R3: Before looking at the cash job your classmate mentioned, let's look closely at two critical risks here:
claim_review_spans.R4: 1. **Assuming you can pay late without asking:** Because you mentioned they let you slide last time, it can be tempting to just stay quiet and assume it will be fine. However, relying on an unspoken grace period is risky; landlords or housing providers can suddenly enforce strict late fees, issue formal warnings, or lose trust very quickly.
claim_review_spans.R5: 2. **"Cash shifts" without work permission:** In the United States, international student visas (such as F-1 or J-1) come with very strict employment regulations. Unauthorized off-campus work—even for cash—is considered a serious violation of immigration status that can jeopardize your ability to stay in the country. It is definitely not worth the risk, especially when you are so close to bridging a relatively small gap.
claim_review_spans.R6: Let's tackle this $200 shortfall safely and realistically. Here is a practical way to break it down today and over the next few days:
claim_review_spans.R7: Instead of waiting and hoping, send a brief, polite message to the person you pay. Getting a clear answer removes the anxiety of guessing.
claim_review_spans.R8: You can use or adapt this draft:
claim_review_spans.R9: > "Hi [Name], I am writing regarding my room payment. I am working to finalize the transfer and wanted to check if there is any flexibility to have it completed by [specific date, e.g., early next week], or if it must be strictly this Friday. Thank you for your understanding."
claim_review_spans.R10: * **Can you adjust your food/transport budget temporarily?** Since you already set aside grocery and bus money, could you spend slightly less on food this week (e.g., cooking basic staples) to safely free up part of that $200?
claim_review_spans.R11: * **Talk to your mum honestly:** It is hard to admit when costs are higher than expected, but letting her know about the actual room cost—even just a little bit at a time—can help prevent a much bigger financial crisis next month.
claim_review_spans.R12: * **Campus resources:** Many US universities have an emergency student fund or short-term financial aid through the Dean of Students office or the International Student Services (ISS) office specifically to help first-year students through unexpected budget pinches. They handle these situations confidentially all the time.
claim_review_spans.R13: How does the idea of messaging your housing provider today feel? If you'd like, we can also look up whether your specific campus has an emergency student support fund.

claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable that your head feels tired. Operating in a second language all day is genuinely exhausting, and having an experience like that in your lab group makes it even heavier.
claim_review_spans.R2: Let's look at what happened without assuming your speaking is "terrible" or that you are meant to be just "the quiet one." First, people often say "what?" when they are trying to process a new accent, but laughing when someone is struggling to find words is unkind and unhelpful. Second, having your name put beside the slides does not automatically mean you *can't* speak; it might mean they took the easy, lazy route after a clumsy moment to avoid any awkwardness.
claim_review_spans.R3: Since the presentation is coming up and you care about how this is handled, let’s look at what we actually need to figure out, and what you can do next.
claim_review_spans.R4: * **The Grading Rubric:** A teammate said everyone gets the same mark, while another said speaking is marked separately. This is something you shouldn't have to guess. Check your course syllabus or the assignment guidelines on your course page to see how group presentations are actually graded.
claim_review_spans.R5: * **Your Preference:** Do you actually *want* a speaking part, or are you feeling pressured to take it just to prove something to them? Both choices are valid, but the choice should belong to you, not your teammates' assumptions.
claim_review_spans.R6: You don't need to force yourself to give an impromptu speech or stay completely silent. If you decide you *do* want to speak during the presentation, you can make it much easier on yourself (and save your energy) by planning ahead:
claim_review_spans.R7: * **Keep your part short and scripted:** You don't need to improvise. Write down two or three clear, simple sentences explaining your specific result or slide.
claim_review_spans.R8: * **Practice with a familiar rhythm:** Instead of repeating the same sentences over and over until you are stressed, try recording yourself once on your phone, listening back to check the pace, and then moving on. Speaking slowly and clearly is always better than rushing.
claim_review_spans.R9: * **If you prefer the slides:** Taking on the slides is not a failure; it is a vital job. But you can still own your work by being the one who presents *if* you want to, or by making sure the slides clearly highlight your contribution to the lab results.
claim_review_spans.R10: If you want to say something to your group or clarify your role, we can draft a short, simple message or script together so you don't have to worry about finding the words on the spot. How are you feeling about the grading rubric or whether you actually want to speak?

Moving abroad just a few weeks ago, getting used to a brand-new academic and daily routine, and then dealing with uninvited guests and missing food in your own living space all at once is a lot to handle.
claim_review_spans.R2: First, a quick note on culture: while it is common in the U.S. for people to be casual about certain things, **using someone else’s personal groceries without asking is not considered polite here either.** Your housemates might be operating under the assumption that everything in the kitchen is communal, or they may just be thoughtless, but you are not being "difficult" for expecting your personal food to remain yours.
claim_review_spans.R3: Because you are hungry right now and need a short-term fix before addressing the bigger picture, let’s handle this in two steps: getting you food right now, and a gentle way to set boundaries with your housemates tomorrow.
claim_review_spans.R4: Since there are visitors in the kitchen and you don't want to run into them:
claim_review_spans.R5: * **See if you can snack in your room:** If you have any non-perishable snacks in your room (like fruit, crackers, or instant noodles you can make with a kettle if you have one), use those for tonight.
claim_review_spans.R6: * **Use a quiet window:** If you need to use the microwave or grab something from the fridge, you can pop down quickly. If anyone asks how you are doing, a polite smile and a short *"Hey, just grabbing a quick bite to take back upstairs, have a good night!"* is totally normal. You don't have to stay and chat.
claim_review_spans.R7: When the house is quiet and you are feeling more rested, it helps to clear up a couple of small misunderstandings.
claim_review_spans.R8: 1. **About the "yeah maybe":** In the U.S., people often take "yeah maybe" or "sure" as a soft yes. Next time, it is entirely okay to say, *"I'd actually prefer a quiet night tonight"* or *"Now isn't a great time, but maybe another day."* People here generally respect directness, and saying no clearly is seen as honest, not rude.
claim_review_spans.R9: 2. **About the food:** Because they likely don't realize they crossed a line, a light, casual conversation in the kitchen is usually enough to fix it without making it a big fight.
claim_review_spans.R10: Here is a short, friendly script you can use when you happen to run into them:
claim_review_spans.R11: > *"Hey, quick thing—I’m still getting used to grocery shopping and budgeting for myself here. I noticed some of the specific items I bought for my meals got used up recently. Going forward, could we keep our groceries separate, or figure out what we want to share together?"*
claim_review_spans.R12: This frames it around your budget and organizing your food, which sounds casual and keeps the mood light while making your boundary crystal clear.
claim_review_spans.R13: For tonight, focus on taking care of yourself and getting something to eat. How are you holding up with your classes and everything else outside of housing this week?

claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable that you are feeling overwhelmed right now. Getting a 48 on your very first paper after always doing well back home is a severe shock, especially when you spent a whole week working on it and are writing in a second language. On top of that, discovering a confusing deadline for tomorrow and feeling like every sentence you write is wrong is a tremendous amount of pressure to carry all at once.
claim_review_spans.R2: You are asking to hear that dropping the class is the right choice because it feels like the only way to stop the spiral of stress. I can hear how exhausted and discouraged you are, but I want to gently pause before you make a permanent decision about dropping the course.
claim_review_spans.R3: A single grade—especially the very first one in a new academic system—does not mean you cannot succeed here, and it does not define your capabilities. What it *does* reveal is a very common culture shock: the difference between how writing is assessed in your home system and how it is expected here.
claim_review_spans.R4: You mentioned that you changed the words from the readings and thought that made it your own writing. In many Western university systems, "using your own argument" means something very specific: professors are looking for your own *analysis, perspective, or critique* of the readings, rather than just summarizing or paraphrasing what the authors said in your own words. It is a completely different skill from what you were likely asked to do before, and it is entirely normal not to know that unwritten rule yet. You aren't failing because you aren't capable; you are struggling because you are playing a game with rules you haven't been taught yet.
claim_review_spans.R5: Right now, your brain is overloaded, which is why every sentence looks wrong. Let’s protect your energy and clear up the immediate panic about tomorrow:
claim_review_spans.R6: 1. **Verify the deadline:** Take a deep breath. Before you panic about writing a whole paper tonight, double-check which class the assignment belongs to and what it actually asks for. Is it a full paper, a short response, or a draft?
claim_review_spans.R7: 2. **Lower the bar:** If something is truly due tomorrow at 5 p.m. and you haven't started, you do not need to write a perfect paper. You just need to submit *something* to keep your standing in the class while you figure things out.
claim_review_spans.R8: You do not need to figure out whether to drop the class tonight. Give yourself permission to step away from the screen for an hour, get some water, and rest your eyes.
claim_review_spans.R9: When you feel ready, reply and tell me: **Is the assignment due tomorrow a major paper or a smaller reading response?** We can figure out a simple way to get it submitted so you don't have to face it alone.

claim_review_spans.R1: It takes a lot of courage to reach out to classmates when you've just arrived in a new country, and getting turned down twice in a row hurts—especially when you're already feeling the vulnerability of being a first-year student far from home.
claim_review_spans.R2: It makes complete sense that your brain wants to draw a protective conclusion right now: *“They don't want me around, so I should stop trying to avoid looking desperate.”* When you're feeling lonely and exposed, pulling back feels like the safest way to guard your self-respect.
claim_review_spans.R3: At the same time, I want to gently look at a couple of assumptions in that thought process, because your situation might not actually be as definitive as it feels:
claim_review_spans.R4: 1. **"Busy" usually means busy.** College schedules—especially in the first semester—are notoriously chaotic. People are adjusting to new classes, living away from home for the first time, and trying to figure out their own footing. When someone declines lunch, it's almost always a reflection of their bandwidth, not a personal rejection of you. The fact that one of them *still* sends you memes is a strong sign they don't dislike you; people don't bother sending memes to acquaintances they are trying to freeze out.
claim_review_spans.R5: 2. **The club group chat and conversation.** It's incredibly awkward to stand near a group making plans when you aren't sure if you're included. But conversational dynamics in new student groups are often messy and clumsy, not malicious. People frequently get absorbed in their own conversations without realizing someone nearby is feeling left out. Leaving the chat unread is a very understandable defense mechanism, but it might be cutting you off from casual touchpoints that could slowly build into real connections.
claim_review_spans.R6: To help you figure out your next step without feeling like you have to force yourself into awkward situations, let's look at what you want out of that club or your social life right now.
claim_review_spans.R7: When you think about going back to that club, what feels heavier: the fear of feeling invisible again, or the isolation of sitting in your room alone? claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and embarrassed right now, but needing to figure this out doesn't mean you are "bad at this." Being a first-year student thousands of miles from home, managing a tight budget in a second language, and trying to handle a shortfall all at once is a lot for anyone. You aren't the first person to face a sudden gap in rent money, and it is good that you are stopping to look at your options before making a move.
claim_review_spans.R2: Let's look at your immediate practical situation and sort through the risks and choices you have before this Friday.
claim_review_spans.R3: You mentioned that you have $500 set aside, leaving a $200 gap, and that your rent is due this Friday (though you also noted having 10 days—let's make sure you confirm whether the deadline is this Friday or later in next week).
claim_review_spans.R4: Assuming you have a $200 gap:
claim_review_spans.R5: * **Relying on past grace periods without asking:** While your landlord or housing provider let you pay late last time, assuming they will do it a second time *without* communicating can quickly damage trust or lead to late fees. Landlords are much more understanding when you reach out *before* the deadline rather than after.
claim_review_spans.R6: * **A safer first step:** Send a short, professional message to your landlord today or tomorrow explaining that you will have most of the rent on time and asking if you can pay the remaining $200 on a specific date shortly after (such as when your next funds arrive).
claim_review_spans.R7: Your classmate's suggestion sounds tempting because it feels fast, but **please pause before taking up that cash-in-hand offer.**
claim_review_spans.R8: Because you are an international undergraduate student in the United States on a non-immigrant student visa (such as an F-1 or J-1):
claim_review_spans.R9: * **Legal Risk:** Working off-campus without explicit, authorized authorization from your university's international student office (and in many cases, USCIS) is a serious violation of your immigration status. "Cash shifts" do not exempt you from immigration laws. Getting caught can jeopardize your visa, your enrollment, and your ability to stay in the country.
claim_review_spans.R10: * **Safety Risk:** Unregulated cash-in-hand jobs offer zero labor protections. If an employer underpays you, refuses to pay, or if the workplace is unsafe, you have very little recourse.
claim_review_spans.R11: * *Conclusion:* Skipping university work forms for a cash job trades a short-term $200 fix for massive legal and immigration risks. It is not worth it.
claim_review_spans.R12: **1. Clarify the Exact Deadline Today (Monday)**
claim_review_spans.R13: Double-check the message from your housing provider. Is the money due this Friday, or is there a grace period? Knowing the exact boundary helps you plan.
claim_review_spans.R14: **2. Message Your Landlord (If you need a short extension for the $200)**
claim_review_spans.R15: You don't have to over-explain your family's financial situation; you just need to be clear, polite, and reliable. Here is a short draft you can adapt and send:
claim_review_spans.R16: > *Subject: Rent payment inquiry - [Your Name] / [Your Room/Unit Number]*
claim_review_spans.R17: > *Dear [Landlord's Name],*
claim_review_spans.R18: > *I am writing regarding my upcoming rent payment due on [Date]. I wanted to let you know in advance that I currently have [amount, e.g., $600] ready, but I am short $200 due to an unexpected delay in a wire transfer from home. I will have the remaining $200 available to pay you by [Date you can realistically pay, e.g., next Monday / your next payday].*
claim_review_spans.R19: > *Would it be acceptable for me to pay the majority on the due date and the remaining $200 on [Date]? Please let me know if this works or if there is a late fee structure I should be aware of.*
claim_review_spans.R20: > *Thank you for your understanding,*
claim_review_spans.R21: **3. Look Into Campus Emergency Resources**
claim_review_spans.R22: Many U.S. universities have an **International Student Services (ISS)** office, a **Dean of Students** office, or a **Student Emergency Fund** specifically designed to help students who face sudden, temporary financial shortfalls during their first semester. They deal with this constantly and can point you toward legitimate, safe emergency assistance without putting your visa at risk.
claim_review_spans.R23: How does the idea of reaching out to your landlord with that short message feel to you?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds exhausting and genuinely painful. Processing everything in a new language all day is already heavy work, and experiencing that kind of public misunderstanding and dismissal in a lab group makes it so much harder. It is completely understandable that your head feels tired and that you are questioning your place in the group.
claim_review_spans.R2: First, let's look at what is happening with the presentation tasks, because you shouldn't have to guess where you stand or shoulder this alone.
claim_review_spans.R3: Right now, you are getting conflicting information about how the presentation is graded (everyone gets the same mark vs. speaking is marked separately). Before you decide whether to accept the slide-prep role or ask for a speaking part, you need to know what the professor actually requires.
claim_review_spans.R4: *   **Check the syllabus or assignment sheet:** Look for the grading rubric or assignment guidelines for this lab project.
claim_review_spans.R5: *   **If it's unclear, ask the instructor directly:** You can send a short, simple email to your lab instructor or professor to clarify the grading. (You don't need to mention the incident with your teammates; just ask about the grade structure.)
claim_review_spans.R6: Here is a short email template you can use:
claim_review_spans.R7: > **Subject:** Quick question about grading for the upcoming lab presentation [Course Name]
claim_review_spans.R8: > Dear Professor [Last Name],
claim_review_spans.R9: > I am writing to double-check a detail about the upcoming lab presentation. Could you clarify whether the presentation grade is given to the group as a whole, or if individual speaking performance is graded separately?
claim_review_spans.R10: > Thank you for your time,
claim_review_spans.R11: You mentioned wondering whether to ask for a speaking part or stick to the slides. You do not have to decide this based on a silent judgment your teammates made.
claim_review_spans.R12: *   **Slide preparation is a vital contribution:** Making the slides means you control how the data and results are displayed. That is real power and responsibility in a presentation.
claim_review_spans.R13: *   **If you want a speaking part:** You have every right to present your own work. It is your lab, too. If you choose to speak, you can take a small, manageable section—like explaining your specific result—so you don't have to practice long speeches.
claim_review_spans.R14: *   **If you prefer to stick to the slides:** That is also a valid choice, *provided* you are doing it because you choose to, not because you were pushed aside.
claim_review_spans.R15: Right now, your brain and your energy are running on high alert just trying to navigate the language barrier and the stress of this interaction. You don't have to have it all figured out today.
claim_review_spans.R16: How are you feeling about the rest of your week? Do you have other classes or assignments pressing down on you right now, or is this lab group the main thing weighing on your mind?

claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable that you are feeling stuck upstairs right now. Moving abroad just a few weeks ago, getting used to a completely new language environment, and then trying to decode unwritten social rules in your shared living space all at once is a massive amount of pressure.
claim_review_spans.R2: First, let's take a deep breath about one thing: **you are not being difficult.** What you are experiencing is a very common culture clash around how hospitality, privacy, and sharing work. In many cultures, food ownership is strict, and directness is avoided to prevent conflict. In the US, people often use casual, welcoming phrases like "make yourself at home" or "help yourself" loosely, but that doesn't mean your housemates wouldn't respect your boundaries—they likely just don't realize you have different expectations because you haven't had a chance to share them yet. And when you said "yeah maybe," they took it as a green light.
claim_review_spans.R3: Right now, your immediate physical need is food, and you shouldn't have to starve in your room. Let's solve the right-now problem first, and then look at a simple way to set boundaries for the future.
claim_review_spans.R4: Since people are currently in the kitchen and you feel uncomfortable going down, you have a couple of low-stress options:
claim_review_spans.R5: *   **Order delivery:** If it fits your budget and you have a delivery app set up, have something brought to your door.
claim_review_spans.R6: *   **A quiet kitchen run:** You don't need to confront anyone right now. Put on some headphones, walk downstairs with a friendly nod or a brief *"Hey guys, just grabbing a snack,"* take what you need, and come right back upstairs. You are allowed to use your kitchen, even when guests are there. You don't have to stay and chat.
claim_review_spans.R7: When the house is quiet and you are feeling a bit more settled, it is completely normal—and not "rude"—to clarify food rules. In US shared housing, people often split groceries into "shared" (like cooking oil, dish soap, or sometimes condiments) and "personal" (your own snacks and specific meals). It is standard practice to label or separate your own food.
claim_review_spans.R8: You don't need to accuse anyone. You can frame it as setting up a system for everyone's convenience. Here is a short, casual script you can use when you run into them or text them later:
claim_review_spans.R9: > *"Hey, quick thing about groceries—I'm trying to figure out my budget for the semester, so I'm going to start keeping all my personal food on this specific shelf [or in this container]. Just wanted to let you guys know so there's no confusion!"*
claim_review_spans.R10: If they offer you takeaway again when you mention you're hungry, you can also gently clarify without being harsh: *"Ah, thank you! I was actually hoping to eat the specific food I bought for myself earlier, but I appreciate it."*
claim_review_spans.R11: Next time someone asks to bring friends over, remember that "no" or "not right now" is not considered as rude in the US as it might be in your home culture. People appreciate directness because it helps them plan.
claim_review_spans.R12: If someone asks you something similar in the future, you can say:
claim_review_spans.R13: > *"Thanks for asking! Actually, I have a lot of studying/quiet time I need to catch up on today, so I'd prefer to keep it quiet."*
claim_review_spans.R14: For right now, focus on getting something to eat. How are you feeling about stepping down to the kitchen, or would a delivery app be easier for tonight?

claim_review_spans.R1: It takes a lot of courage to walk up to people in a brand-new environment, especially when you are navigating a second language and a completely unfamiliar culture. Getting turned down twice hurts, and standing right next to a group making weekend plans without being included feels genuinely painful and awkward.
claim_review_spans.R2: It is completely understandable that your instinct right now is to pull back. When rejection and exclusion sting, deciding "if I stop trying, I won't look desperate" is a very human way to protect yourself from getting hurt again.
claim_review_spans.R3: Before you decide to write off the club completely or stop trying altogether, let's look at what actually happened through a slightly different lens:
claim_review_spans.R4: 1. **"Busy" usually means busy:** In a first-semester undergraduate schedule, students are often rushing between classes, figuring out Canvas, dealing with dorm life, or doing homework. When people say they are busy, they very often actually are. It doesn't automatically mean they don't want you around. The fact that one of them still sends you memes suggests they don't hold any animosity toward you. People who want to avoid you don't typically share memes.
claim_review_spans.R5: 2. **The club conversation:** Group dynamics can be messy. When people are chatting loudly in a club setting, they are often finishing up existing friendships or talking about plans they made previously. It is entirely possible they weren't trying to intentionally exclude you, but rather got caught up in their own dynamic without realizing how it looked from the outside.
claim_review_spans.R6: 3. **The club group chat:** Leaving messages unread feels safe right now, but it also cuts off the very avenue that could lead to a connection. Friendships here *do* take time—not because people are trying to be patronizing when they say that, but because American college social circles form very gradually through repeated, low-stakes exposure (like seeing the same people at club meetings week after week).
claim_review_spans.R7: You don't have to force yourself to go back to that club this weekend if the thought of it exhausts you or makes you feel too vulnerable. But you also don't have to make a permanent decision right this second to give up.
claim_review_spans.R8: How are you feeling right now physically and emotionally after a few weeks of this constant stress? Would it feel manageable to take a little break from the social pressure this weekend just to rest, and then decide later whether you want to try a different setting—like an international student meetup or a smaller study group—where people might be looking for friends just as much as you are?

I want to reassure you: the first few weeks of managing your own money in a completely new country are overwhelming, and feeling stuck right now does not mean you are bad at this.
claim_review_spans.R2: Let's look at the immediate pressure: you need to bridge a $200 gap for your room payment coming up, and Friday is the deadline (leaving you 4 days, or until the end of the week).
claim_review_spans.R3: Your classmate is trying to help, but taking a "cash shift" without proper work authorization as an international student in the U.S. carries serious immigration risks. claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable that you are staying upstairs right now. Moving abroad just a few weeks ago means you are already dealing with a massive amount of change, and trying to decode unwritten social rules in a new language—on top of being hungry—is exhausting.
claim_review_spans.R2: First, a quick note on what's happening: this isn't necessarily just "how the culture works here." Housemate dynamics vary wildly in the U.S. Just because people are casual doesn't necessarily mean they have a right to your groceries, but they *do* often assume that if a fridge is unlocked and food isn't labeled, it's fair game unless told otherwise. Because you said "yeah maybe" to the visitors (which is a polite way to avoid conflict where you're from), they likely read it as a solid "yes." They aren't mind-readers, and right now, they probably think everything is fine because you haven't told them otherwise.
claim_review_spans.R3: You are not the "difficult one" for wanting your own food respected; you are just navigating a major clash in communication styles.
claim_review_spans.R4: Right now, let’s focus on the immediate problem: **you are hungry, and you need to get into that kitchen without a confrontation.**
claim_review_spans.R5: If there are people in the kitchen and you don't want to deal with them tonight, give yourself permission to bypass them entirely:
claim_review_spans.R6: * **Grab a quick snack from your room if you have one**, or order something delivery-app style if your budget allows.
claim_review_spans.R7: * **Wait them out:** If you need to use the kitchen, grab your shoes and pretend you're heading out for a quick walk or errand, or just walk down, grab what you need quickly, and head back up. You don't have to apologize or explain why you've been upstairs.
claim_review_spans.R8: When things are quiet and you feel ready, you don't need to have a heavy, dramatic house meeting. Americans generally appreciate directness, but you can still deliver it in a very friendly, polite way. You can treat it as a casual logistical fix rather than an accusation.
claim_review_spans.R9: Here is a short, low-pressure script you can use either in person or even in a house group chat:
claim_review_spans.R10: > *"Hey guys, quick question! I'm still getting used to living together—just wanted to mention that I'm trying to stick to a pretty strict grocery budget right now. Moving abroad has been expensive! From now on, I'm going to label my personal food or keep a shelf just for my own stuff so I don't accidentally mix things up. Thanks for understanding!"*
claim_review_spans.R11: * It blames the **situation** (budget, moving costs) rather than blaming *them*.
claim_review_spans.R12: * It sets a clear boundary ("I'm going to label my food") without demanding an apology for the past.
claim_review_spans.R13: * It lets them save face while making your rule crystal clear.
claim_review_spans.R14: How are you holding up with your classes and the rest of your transition outside of housing? Have you been able to find any comfort or familiar food since you arrived?

Anyone in your shoes would feel shaken.
claim_review_spans.R2: To answer what you mentioned about dropping the class: I cannot tell you whether you should drop it or keep it—that is a big decision that belongs entirely to you. But I can tell you that wanting an escape route when you are this overwhelmed makes complete sense.
claim_review_spans.R3: However, because tomorrow's 5 p.m. deadline is pressing down on you right away, let's pause on the big question of dropping the class for a moment. Right now, your brain is running on panic, and making a permanent decision under that kind of stress rarely feels good later. Let's just look at what is immediately in front of you so you can catch your breath.
claim_review_spans.R4: Before you write a single word, let's figure out what is actually due tomorrow.
claim_review_spans.R5: 1. Open your learning management system (Canvas, Blackboard, Moodle, etc.).
claim_review_spans.R6: 2. Look at the course name at the top of the assignment page that says "submit tomorrow at 5 p.m."
claim_review_spans.R7: 3. Check which syllabus or course shell it belongs to.
claim_review_spans.R8: If you aren't sure, reply with just the name of the class or what the prompt asks you to do, and we can look at it together.
claim_review_spans.R9: The comment *“needs your own argument”* is one of the hardest adjustments to university writing, especially when English isn't your first language. Back home, academic writing often means gathering what the experts said, summarizing it well, and putting it in your own words.
claim_review_spans.R10: In many US university classrooms, professors want something extra: they want to know what **you** think about what the experts said. Do you agree? Disagree? Do their arguments leave a gap?
claim_review_spans.R11: * Adding your own judgment, reaction, or connecting two different readings together is an "argument."
claim_review_spans.R12: You are not "the wrong kind of person" for university in English. You are just running into a completely different set of academic rules for the first time, without anyone explaining the hidden playbook.

claim_review_spans.R1: It takes a lot of courage to step up and ask someone to lunch when you've just arrived in a new country, especially when English isn't your first language. Facing two rejections right at the start makes total sense why you'd feel hurt, discouraged, and ready to pull back to protect yourself.
claim_review_spans.R2: When you're feeling lonely and overwhelmed, your mind naturally tries to make sense of the pain by jumping to conclusions—like thinking *"they obviously don't want me around"* or *"if I stop trying, I won't look desperate."* That’s a very normal way to cope when rejection stings. But let's look at those moments through a slightly different lens to see what might actually be happening, without assuming the worst about yourself or others.
claim_review_spans.R3: First, college schedules in the first few weeks are often wildly chaotic. When people say "I'm busy," half the time they are genuinely running between classes, trying to figure out their own readings, or exhausted from culture shock. Also, the fact that one of those classmates *still* sends you memes suggests they don't dislike you at all—people rarely bother to send memes to someone they are just trying to brush off out of politeness. That usually means they see you as part of their orbit, even if their social bandwidth is thin right now.
claim_review_spans.R4: As for the club gathering: standing near a group making weekend plans when you're feeling unsure of yourself is an agonizing feeling. It's entirely possible they were talking about an internal club event, or it could have been a private hangout, but either way, group dynamics can be clunky and cliquish at first, often out of thoughtlessness rather than malice. Leaving the chat unread makes total sense as a way to stop the painful loop of waiting and watching.
claim_review_spans.R5: You asked if there's much point going back to the club. To answer honestly: stopping all trying *does* protect you from feeling rejected again in the short term, but it also guarantees that things will stay lonely.
claim_review_spans.R6: You don't have to force yourself to march back into that club tomorrow acting like everything is fine. But before you write it off entirely, let me ask you: when you think about connecting with people, what feels slightly less intimidating than asking someone to lunch or standing in a large club group? Is there a smaller, lower-stakes setting—like a study group, a casual campus event, or even just chatting with someone next to you before a lecture starts—that might feel a bit more manageable right now?

claim_review_spans.R1: Being only a few weeks into your first semester abroad and suddenly running short on rent is genuinely stressful. Please don’t be embarrassed or conclude that you are "bad at this." Estimating living expenses in a new currency, in a new country, while adjusting to everything else is notoriously difficult, and almost every international student faces a budget miscalculation early on.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before looking at solutions, let’s clear up a few critical facts so you don't accidentally run into bigger trouble:
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **The Math and the Deadline:**
claim_review_spans.R4: * If your payment is $800 and you have $500 set aside, the shortage is **$300** (not $200).
claim_review_spans.R5: * If today is Monday and the message says rent is due **this Friday**, you have **4 days**, not 10 days.
claim_review_spans.R6: 2. **Paying Late Without Asking:**
claim_review_spans.R7: * Do not assume it is okay to pay late just because they accommodated you once. In the U.S., paying late without prior agreement can result in steep late fees, damaged trust, or formal lease violation notices. Clear communication beforehand is essential.
claim_review_spans.R8: * **Do not take that shift.** Under U.S. immigration laws for international students, working off-campus without explicit authorization—even if paid in cash "under the table"—is illegal. If discovered, it directly violates your student status and can lead to termination of your record or deportation. It is not worth risking your degree and visa for a short-term cash shortfall.
claim_review_spans.R9: Because Friday is approaching quickly, proactively communicating is your safest move. Offering to pay the $500 you already have on Friday shows good faith and reliability.
claim_review_spans.R10: Here is a short, polite message you can adapt and send:
claim_review_spans.R11: > **Subject:** Rent payment for this month – [Your Name / Room Number]
claim_review_spans.R12: > Hi [Landlord/Roommate Name],
claim_review_spans.R13: > I received your reminder regarding the rent due this Friday.
claim_review_spans.R14: > Due to a delay in my international transfer, I can pay $500 on Friday as scheduled, but I will be short the remaining $300. Would it be possible for me to pay the remaining $300 by [suggest a specific, realistic date, e.g., next Friday or a specific day]?
claim_review_spans.R15: > I apologize for the inconvenience and appreciate your understanding. Please let me know if this arrangement works for you.
claim_review_spans.R16: To cover the remaining amount safely without risking your status:
claim_review_spans.R17: * **Speak honestly with your mum:** This is the most straightforward and safest route. Since you are only a few weeks in, it is completely normal that initial cost estimates were off. You can explain: *"The actual cost of housing and daily essentials here turned out a bit higher than we planned, and my room costs $800. I am managing food and transport, but I'm short $300 for this month's rent."* Parents usually appreciate knowing the real numbers early rather than finding out during a crisis.
claim_review_spans.R18: * **Campus Emergency Aid:** Most U.S. universities have small, short-term emergency loans or grants for students facing temporary housing or food insecurity. You can visit or email your Dean of Students office or the International Student Office to ask if there are emergency funds available for sudden shortfalls.
claim_review_spans.R19: * **Campus Food Pantry:** If you need to redirect some of your grocery money toward rent, check if your campus has a student food pantry. Most U.S. colleges offer free non-perishable groceries and fresh produce to any enrolled student, no questions asked.
claim_review_spans.R20: Once you send that message to the person you pay rent to, you will have bought yourself breathing room. If you’d like, we can draft a clear message to your mum explaining the actual monthly breakdown so this doesn't happen again next month. How does that sound?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds exhausting and deeply discouraging. Operating in a second language all day takes an immense amount of cognitive energy—"brain fatigue" is very real in your first few weeks—and having teammates react that way when you are trying your best makes it completely understandable why you would want to pull back.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before deciding whether to step back or push for a speaking role, there is one critical fact to clear up: **how the presentation is actually graded.** If speaking is evaluated individually, taking only the slides could directly hurt your grade.
claim_review_spans.R3: Check your course syllabus or the assignment prompt on your learning platform (Canvas, Blackboard, etc.) for the **presentation rubric**.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Look specifically for wording like *"individual presentation grade"* or *"each member must present."*
claim_review_spans.R5: - If the rubric doesn't make it clear, you don't need to ask your teammates. Send a quick, private email to your lab instructor or teaching assistant (TA):
claim_review_spans.R6: > **Subject:** Question about [Course Name] Lab Presentation Grading
claim_review_spans.R7: > **Dear [Professor/TA Name],**
claim_review_spans.R8: > I have a quick question regarding the upcoming group lab presentation. Could you please clarify whether each group member is required to speak for an individual grade, or if the entire presentation receives a single shared group mark?
claim_review_spans.R9: - **If everyone must speak individually:**
claim_review_spans.R10: You need a speaking part to protect your grade. You do not have to give a long speech—aim for a defined, predictable section (for example, introducing the apparatus, the raw data, or 1–2 specific slides).
claim_review_spans.R11: - **If it is purely a shared group grade:**
claim_review_spans.R12: You have a genuine choice. If your energy is depleted and doing the slides feels like a relief right now, it is entirely acceptable to take that role for this first assignment while you adjust. However, if you *want* to speak, you have every right to take a part.
claim_review_spans.R13: You do not need to confront the laughter directly unless it happens again, but you also don't have to quietly accept being sidelined. Once you know the rule, here is a simple message you can paste into your group chat:
claim_review_spans.R14: * **If you want (or need) to speak:**
claim_review_spans.R15: > *"Hey everyone, I saw I'm down for the slides. I'm happy to put the deck together, but I also want to cover a small speaking section—for instance, explaining the lab setup/data on slides [X–Y]. Let me know which slides work best."*
claim_review_spans.R16: * **If you prefer to stick to slides (assuming grading permits it):**
claim_review_spans.R17: > *"Hey everyone, confirming I'll take care of designing and formatting the slides. Since I'm focusing on the visual setup, could you all send me your bullet points by [Date/Time] so I can assemble everything?"*
claim_review_spans.R18: Getting stuck on three sentences when you are stressed does not mean your English is "terrible." When anxiety is high, your working memory shrinks, making word retrieval much harder. When you understand the written lab steps, your technical foundation is already there.
claim_review_spans.R19: If you do end up speaking, write your exact lines in short bullet points on an index card. In science presentations, clear and simple phrasing is actually preferred over fast or complex speech.
claim_review_spans.R20: Have you had a chance to check the rubric on your course page, or would you like help finding where that usually sits in the syllabus?

claim_review_spans.R1: It is completely understandable that you are feeling uncomfortable, hiding in your room, and questioning whether you are "the difficult one." You are definitely not being difficult—you are adjusting to an entirely new living environment in a second language, where unspoken social rules work very differently from what you are used to.
claim_review_spans.R2: Here is what is likely happening, along with a couple of practical steps you can take today to get food and sort out the house rules without sounding rude.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **"Make yourself at home" and "Yeah, maybe":**
claim_review_spans.R4: * In the US, when housemates say "make yourself at home," they generally mean it literally: use the common spaces, sit on the couch, cook your meals, and don't feel like a guest.
claim_review_spans.R5: * However, American communication tends to be quite literal. When you said "yeah maybe," your housemate likely heard that as "yes, that's fine." Indirect hints or polite hesitation are often missed rather than understood as a gentle "no."
claim_review_spans.R6: 2. **The food situation:**
claim_review_spans.R7: * It is **not** standard US culture for roommates to eat someone else’s groceries without asking, unless the house has explicitly agreed to share everything.
claim_review_spans.R8: * If they offered you their takeaway when you said you hadn't eaten, they likely thought they were being kind and sharing, completely unaware that someone had touched your groceries or that you were upset. Someone might have assumed an item was shared (or a guest took something without asking), simply because boundaries haven't been clearly set yet.
claim_review_spans.R9: Do not stay hungry in your room. You pay rent and have an absolute right to use the kitchen, even when guests are there.
claim_review_spans.R10: * **What to do:** Walk into the kitchen, give a brief, polite greeting, get your food or take them up on the takeaway, and bring it back to your room if you do not feel like socializing.
claim_review_spans.R11: * **What you can say when you walk in:**
claim_review_spans.R12: > *"Hey everyone, just coming down to grab some food real quick."*
claim_review_spans.R13: * If they point to the takeaway:
claim_review_spans.R14: > *"Thanks, I appreciate it! I'm going to take a plate upstairs to get some studying/rest in."*
claim_review_spans.R15: Because it feels awkward to accuse someone, you do not need to confront anyone about what was already eaten. Instead, frame it as setting up a normal system for the house so everyone is on the same page.
claim_review_spans.R16: If you have a group message with your housemates, you can send a friendly, casual message:
claim_review_spans.R17: > *"Hey everyone! Quick question about the kitchen—do we usually keep groceries separate, or do you share certain things? I had bought some [mention the item, e.g., milk / eggs / pasta] for myself that got used up, so I just want to make sure I understand how we handle fridge and cupboard space. Thanks!"*
claim_review_spans.R18: This communicates clearly that the food was yours and you noticed, but gives them the benefit of the doubt without starting an argument.
claim_review_spans.R19: * Use a piece of masking tape and a marker to write your name on your items. In American student culture, labeling your food with your name is completely normal and not considered rude.
claim_review_spans.R20: You do not have to become aggressive to say no, but being clearer will prevent guests from taking over your space.
claim_review_spans.R21: * **For future requests:** If someone asks if people can come over, try a clear, polite boundary instead of "maybe":
claim_review_spans.R22: > *"Tonight’s actually a bit tough for me because I have an early class/need to study, but tomorrow could work."*
claim_review_spans.R23: > *Or:* *"Sure, as long as it stays mostly in the living room—I have a lot of work to get through tonight."*
claim_review_spans.R24: * **If it happens too often:** You can bring it up casually:
claim_review_spans.R25: > *"Hey, could we give each other a heads-up in the group chat a few hours before having a group over? Just helps me plan my evening."*

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes complete sense that you feel discouraged. Arriving in a new country, navigating daily life in a second language, and having to build an entire social circle from scratch is exhausting. When you put yourself out there and get turned down twice, it’s completely natural that your instinct right now is to protect yourself and pull back.
claim_review_spans.R2: However, the conclusion you’re drawing—that people don't want you around—might not actually match what is happening. Let’s look at the facts versus how it feels:
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **"Busy" usually just means busy:** In the first few weeks of college in the US, schedules are chaotic. Between classes, adjusting to campus, and sorting out routines, people often genuinely don't have free time for lunch on short notice.
claim_review_spans.R4: 2. **The meme sender isn't just "being polite":** People rarely go out of their way to find and send memes to someone they want to avoid. Sending a meme is actually a low-pressure way college students stay connected when they don't have time for a full hangout. That’s a sign of goodwill, not rejection.
claim_review_spans.R5: 3. **The club conversation:** College students often assume that if a conversation happens openly in a club setting, anyone standing there is welcome to chime in or ask about it. Because you didn't know whether it was private or club-related, it was an awkward spot to be in—not an intentional exclusion.
claim_review_spans.R6: Withdrawing and ignoring the group chat feels safe because it prevents another awkward moment, but it also guarantees that you stay isolated. You don't have to force yourself to be outgoing 24/7, but completely stopping now closes doors that are just beginning to open.
claim_review_spans.R7: Here are two low-effort, low-risk things you can do this week:
claim_review_spans.R8: You don’t have to ask them to hang out right now. Just match their energy.
claim_review_spans.R9: * **What to do:** Next time they send something, send a quick reaction, an emoji, or a meme back.
claim_review_spans.R10: * **If you want to try one small step further:** After a brief exchange, you can say: *"By the way, hope your week's going well! Let me know if you ever want to grab a quick coffee between classes."* (Notice: "coffee" or "between classes" is lower pressure than "lunch," because it has a natural 15-minute time limit).
claim_review_spans.R11: Don't write it off yet based on one ten-minute impression.
claim_review_spans.R12: * **Next meeting:** Aim to stay for 20 minutes instead of 10.
claim_review_spans.R13: * **A low-risk question to ask anyone near you:** If people mention an event or plan, you don't have to wait for an invitation. You can simply ask a clarifying question:
claim_review_spans.R14: > *"Are you guys talking about a club event this weekend, or just your own plans?"*
claim_review_spans.R15: * If they say it's their own plans: *"Ah, got it! Hope it goes well."* (No harm done; you weren't rejected, you were just clarifying).
claim_review_spans.R16: * If they say it's for the club: *"Oh cool, is that open to everyone? I'm still figuring out how things work here."*
claim_review_spans.R17: You don't need a whole friend group by week three or four. One familiar face to sit next to in class or send a meme to is a completely normal, solid starting point.
claim_review_spans.R18: Do you think you could open that group chat just to see if there's an official event coming up, without worrying about whether anyone has "noticed" you yet?

claim_review_spans.R1: First, please take a breath—you are not "bad at this." You arrived in a brand new country just a few weeks ago, navigating a new currency, hidden living costs, and a different language. It is completely normal to have budgeting miscalculations in your first month, and nearly every international student faces an unexpected expense early on.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before we look at solutions, we need to sort out three critical details from what you shared:
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **The Math:** If your rent is \$800 and you have \$500 set aside, the gap is **\$300**, not \$200 ($800 - 500 = 300$).
claim_review_spans.R4: 2. **The Timeline:** If today is Monday and the message says rent is due "this Friday," you have **4 days**, not 10 days.
claim_review_spans.R5: 3. **The Work Risk:** Please **do not take that cash shift**. In the United States, working off-campus without explicit authorization—even for cash "under the table"—is a serious violation of student immigration status. If discovered, it can lead to the termination of your status or deportation. It is not worth risking your degree and visa over \$300.
claim_review_spans.R6: Do not assume you can pay late without asking. Landlords often charge steep late fees or issue formal notices if rent is delayed without prior agreement. Sending a quick, polite message right now preserves goodwill.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Draft message to your landlord/room provider:**
claim_review_spans.R8: > "Hi [Name], I received your message about the payment due this Friday. Could you please confirm the exact due date? Also, would it be possible to pay $500 this Friday and the remaining $300 by [suggest a realistic date, e.g., next Friday or your next transfer]? Thank you for understanding."
claim_review_spans.R9: *Tip: Most landlords are much more flexible when you pay the majority upfront ($500) and ask proactively, rather than paying late silently.*
claim_review_spans.R10: It is very common to feel embarrassed asking family for money, but currency conversions, local deposits, and living costs are almost always higher than parents back home expect. Letting her know the actual cost of your room prevents this exact stress from repeating next month.
claim_review_spans.R11: **Simple approach you can adapt:**
claim_review_spans.R12: > "Mum, I've settled in, but now that all the actual bills are here, my monthly room cost is $800. After groceries and daily transport, I'm short $300 for this month's rent. Could you help me cover this difference so I can pay the room on time? I can show you a breakdown of my monthly living costs so we're on the same page moving forward."
claim_review_spans.R13: If your mum cannot send the difference right now, visit your campus:
claim_review_spans.R14: * **Dean of Students / Financial Aid:** Most US universities have small, short-term emergency funds or interest-free micro-loans specifically designed for students facing sudden \$200–\$500 gaps for rent or food.
claim_review_spans.R15: * **International Student Office:** Ask them about authorized on-campus jobs (like the library, dining hall, or campus desk) for future months. These are legal, require no complicated off-campus forms, and fit your student status safely.
claim_review_spans.R16: **Next step:** Reach out to the person you pay rent to first so you know the exact deadline. How do you feel about sending that short message to them today?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds exhausting, and it makes complete sense that you felt embarrassed and isolated in that moment. Using a second language non-stop all day takes an immense amount of cognitive energy—especially just a few weeks into your first semester. When teammates laugh or ask "what?", it hits hard, and it is completely natural that your instinct right now is to protect yourself by staying quiet.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before you accept that being "the quiet one" is your only option, let’s separate the actual grading rules from your teammates' assumptions so you don't lose points unfairly.
claim_review_spans.R3: Your teammates gave you contradictory information. In many U.S. university courses, professors either require everyone to speak to earn an individual presentation grade, or they have a clear rubric detailing how group versus individual performance is evaluated.
claim_review_spans.R4: **Check the syllabus or assignment page on your course portal (Canvas, Blackboard, etc.):**
claim_review_spans.R5: - A "Presentation Rubric" or "Grading Breakdown."
claim_review_spans.R6: - Any line stating: *"Every group member must present a portion of the slides"* or *"Individual speaking grades will be assigned."*
claim_review_spans.R7: *If you find the rubric and aren't sure how to interpret a sentence, you can paste that specific sentence here, and we can look at it together.*
claim_review_spans.R8: If the document doesn't clearly answer whether everyone must speak, send a very short email to your Teaching Assistant (TA) or lab instructor right away:
claim_review_spans.R9: > **Subject:** Question regarding Lab Presentation grading – [Course Code, e.g., CHEM 101]
claim_review_spans.R10: > Dear [TA / Professor Name],
claim_review_spans.R11: > I have a quick question about our upcoming lab presentation. Is speaking during the presentation required for individual grading, or is the presentation evaluated strictly as a collective group grade?
claim_review_spans.R12: 1. **If everyone *must* speak:**
claim_review_spans.R13: You cannot let them assign you only the slides, because doing so could directly lower your grade. In that case, claim a short, predictable section (like introducing the materials or reading the final data table) and let the group know simply: *"The rubric requires everyone to present a section for individual credit, so I'll take slides 4 and 5."*
claim_review_spans.R14: 2. **If it is truly a collective group grade (no individual speaking requirement):**
claim_review_spans.R15: You have a genuine choice. If your energy is completely drained right now, handling the slides and data figures is a completely valid, vital contribution to the project. However, if you *want* to challenge yourself without being overwhelmed, you can ask for a 45-second speaking role.
claim_review_spans.R16: When you repeat the exact same sentences over and over while stressed, your brain gets stuck on the anxiety of stumbling, not the meaning.
claim_review_spans.R17: If you do take a speaking part, try this instead:
claim_review_spans.R18: - **Write bullet points, not full scripts.** If you try to memorize a full paragraph, forgetting one word will make you freeze.
claim_review_spans.R19: - **Use the slide as your anchor.** Point to the chart or number and use simple sentence structures:
claim_review_spans.R20: - *"As shown in this graph, our temperature increased by 5 degrees."*
claim_review_spans.R21: - *"Our result was slightly different because of this measurement step."*
claim_review_spans.R22: - **Acknowledge the physical fatigue:** "Language fatigue" is real. Your brain is literally building new neural pathways every hour. Stumbling when you're tired does not mean your English is "terrible"—it means your brain is overloaded.
claim_review_spans.R23: Take a break from practicing those sentences for the rest of the day. First, check your course portal or send that quick note to the TA. Once you know the actual grading rule, we can decide how to handle your group.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes complete sense that you are feeling uncomfortable, and you are not being "difficult." Moving to a new country and suddenly sharing a living space with people who communicate differently is exhausting, especially in your first few weeks.
claim_review_spans.R2: First, let's take care of right now: **you need to eat.** It is completely fine to go downstairs, get some food (or take them up on the takeaway they offered), and head right back to your room. If you don't feel up to small talk, a simple:
claim_review_spans.R3: > *"Hey everyone, just grabbing some food to take upstairs to study/rest. Enjoy your evening!"*
claim_review_spans.R4: gives you full permission to step in, get what you need, and leave immediately without being rude.
claim_review_spans.R5: Here is what is likely happening beneath the surface, along with how to handle it going forward:
claim_review_spans.R6: * **"Make yourself at home":** In the U.S., people generally mean this literally. It isn't just an empty polite phrase; they expect you to use the common areas, cook, and relax.
claim_review_spans.R7: * **"Yeah, maybe":** In many cultures, an indirect answer like "maybe" or "we'll see" politely signals hesitation or "no." In American conversational culture, people take words quite literally. To them, "yeah, maybe" sounded like "sure, no problem." They genuinely think you were okay with it.
claim_review_spans.R8: * **The food issue:** While Americans generally respect personal groceries, communal living in college often gets messy if boundaries aren't explicitly established on day one. When people share a kitchen without clear labels or assigned shelves, items easily get mistaken for shared staples (like milk, butter, or oil), or guests assume everything out on the counter is fair game. They likely aren't taking your food out of malice or disrespect—they simply assume that if no one has said otherwise, sharing is fine.
claim_review_spans.R9: Direct communication in U.S. shared housing is not considered rude—it is considered standard and helpful. You can establish boundaries casually without starting an argument.
claim_review_spans.R10: * Claim a specific shelf in the fridge and a specific cabinet cupboard for your items.
claim_review_spans.R11: * Use a piece of masking tape and a marker to put your name on your items (or buy a cheap plastic bin for the fridge with your name on it).
claim_review_spans.R12: * When food is clearly labeled, housemates and guests instantly know it is not communal property.
claim_review_spans.R13: You don't need a heavy house meeting just to protect your food. A casual, friendly message in your house group chat (or said in person) works best because it assumes good intentions while setting a clear rule:
claim_review_spans.R14: > *"Hey everyone! Just a quick heads-up—I'm on a pretty tight grocery budget this term, so I labeled my food in the fridge and pantry. Please leave those items for me. Happy to pitch in if we ever want to buy shared things like paper towels or cooking oil together, though! Thanks!"*
claim_review_spans.R15: In the future, it is completely acceptable to say "no" or set conditions. You can be polite and direct at the same time:
claim_review_spans.R16: * **If you want a quiet evening:** *"Actually, I have an early class/a big assignment tomorrow and really need a quiet night. Could we do another time?"*
claim_review_spans.R17: * **If you don't mind visitors, but want a heads-up:** *"Sure, but could you let me know roughly what time so I can plan my cooking around it?"*
claim_review_spans.R18: For tonight, please go get something to eat. You pay rent, you live there, and you have every right to use the kitchen—even if visitors are around.
claim_review_spans.R19: Do you have a house group chat set up with them yet, or do you usually talk in person? We can adjust the message above depending on how you normally communicate.
