claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful and isolating—especially so early after arriving, when you’re already adjusting and trying to read social cues in a new language/culture. I also want to gently challenge one part: two classmates being “busy” isn’t enough evidence to conclude “they don’t want you around,” and mixed signals (memes, chatting near you, not explicitly inviting you) can have a lot of innocent explanations.
claim_review_spans.R2: - **You asked on the wrong days / wrong moment.** “Busy” is often just that they can’t do lunch *then*, not a personal rejection.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Group dynamics:** some people talk plans around others without thinking about whether it’s an invitation.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **They assume you’re okay alone / don’t want to bother you.** If you’re not joining conversations, they may not know you want to be included.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **Language/cue uncertainty:** they may not realize you’re unsure, or they may assume you’ll read between the lines.
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Memes can be friendly, not just polite.** People often do small friendly gestures even when they’re not ready for full invitations.
claim_review_spans.R7: Not yet. Based on what you wrote, the club is currently one of your best chances to build connections—it’s also where the “evidence” is mixed. Quitting now would remove your fastest opportunity to test whether you can belong there.
claim_review_spans.R8: A better goal than “stop trying” is: **make it easier for people to include you** with clearer, low-pressure invitations.
claim_review_spans.R9: Instead of waiting for someone to invite you, aim for **one direct but casual line** that doesn’t require them to “read your intention.”
claim_review_spans.R10: > “Hey, I’m trying to find something to do on Saturday. Are you going anywhere with the club or friends?”
claim_review_spans.R11: > “I’m going to grab coffee after this—want to come?”
claim_review_spans.R12: > “I’m new here—does anyone want to meet up on Saturday? Even just something small.”
claim_review_spans.R13: Then do something important: **choose a response window**. If nobody answers in, say, 24 hours, you send *one follow-up* or you try the same tone in person next time. You’re not “waiting for someone to notice you”; you’re initiating and then reading what happens.
claim_review_spans.R14: Unread doesn’t automatically mean “they think you’re desperate.” But it does mean you’re protecting yourself from rejection—and that protection is making you feel worse.
claim_review_spans.R15: - Then let it be awkward for a moment. That’s normal when you’re new.
claim_review_spans.R16: 1) When you asked people for lunch, did you say it in a super casual way (“Want to grab lunch sometime?”) or more specific (“today at 1?”)?
claim_review_spans.R17: 2) Roughly how many people were at the club gathering, and did you manage to speak to anyone briefly (even small talk)?
claim_review_spans.R18: If you answer those, I can suggest exactly what kind of invitation will feel most natural in your situation—and help you draft a message you can post that won’t make you feel exposed.

claim_review_spans.R1: First—I’m really glad you wrote this out. What you’re describing sounds stressful, but also very solvable. This isn’t a “you’re bad at money” problem; it’s a timing + information + embarrassment problem.
claim_review_spans.R2: You have **one concrete deadline**: the remaining **$200** by **Friday** (10 days?—but they said due Friday, and it’s Monday now, so effectively **4 days** to pay unless you negotiate).
claim_review_spans.R3: Also, I need to gently flag one risk: **don’t assume** “cash shifts = no work permission needed.” In the US, whether you can legally work depends on your **visa status and what kind of work it is**, and cash-in-hand arrangements can still cause problems (and scams are common). Let’s focus on safer options first.
claim_review_spans.R4: Message the housing/room payment person **today**. Don’t over-explain—just confirm options.
claim_review_spans.R5: > Hi, I’m sorry for the confusion—my next payment is due this Friday. I’m able to pay **$200** to cover the remaining balance by Friday. Would that work for the late/partial payment, or do you prefer another arrangement? If you allow late payment, I can pay the rest on **[specific day]**.
claim_review_spans.R6: If they allow late last time, this is still worth asking **once clearly**. It reduces panic and preserves your relationship.
claim_review_spans.R7: Make a small, realistic list and pick 1–2 tonight:
claim_review_spans.R8: - **Ask Mom for a top-up immediately**: even a partial transfer for this Friday. (You don’t have to disclose every detail—just that there’s a shortfall this week.)
claim_review_spans.R9: - **Borrow temporarily** from a friend/classmate (even $200 for 1–2 weeks) and set a repayment date.
claim_review_spans.R10: - **Use any emergency funds** you already have (even if it’s not ideal).
claim_review_spans.R11: - **Check if your school offers small emergency grants/aid** (some schools have them, and you can ask without it affecting grades immediately—just ask the right office).
claim_review_spans.R12: If you tell me whether your “Mum sent less money” happened because of a transfer delay vs. because she budgeted lower, I can help you choose the most persuasive wording.
claim_review_spans.R13: It might feel “easier than school forms,” but for international students this is where people get burned. Here’s the practical approach:
claim_review_spans.R14: - **Don’t go start anything** until you know what’s legal for your specific status.
claim_review_spans.R15: - Even if classmates say it’s fine, it doesn’t reliably protect you.
claim_review_spans.R16: - If you want, we can look for the **right campus office question** to ask so you get a clear answer quickly.
claim_review_spans.R17: **Safest immediate plan:** treat the cash shift as a “later backup,” not your primary fix before Friday.
claim_review_spans.R18: Do you have any way to send/get **$200 by Friday** other than the cash shifts—like a transfer from your mom, a loan from a friend, or any remaining funds you haven’t counted yet?
claim_review_spans.R19: If you answer that, I’ll help you pick the fastest path and draft the exact messages (to the room payer and/or to your mum).

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful—especially in a lab group where you’re already under pressure to understand everything *and* express it in English. From what you described, I think you’re dealing with two separate issues at once:
claim_review_spans.R2: 1) **You had a real communication moment** that didn’t go smoothly (accent/word-finding made things harder).
claim_review_spans.R3: 2) **You’re interpreting that moment as a decision about your “place” in the group** (“they decided I can’t speak / I should just avoid speaking”).
claim_review_spans.R4: It might be true, but it also might be a *misunderstanding or a lack of confidence from them*, not a permanent judgment about you.
claim_review_spans.R5: Even if the group mark is the same for everyone, **some rubrics still evaluate presentation components** (clarity, explanation, Q&A, etc.). So avoiding speaking doesn’t guarantee a better outcome—it could actually cost you points *and* make your next group harder.
claim_review_spans.R6: Here’s a script you can use (simple, non-confrontational):
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I felt nervous yesterday explaining. I can contribute—could I be responsible for a small part like explaining my method/result for 1–2 slides? If my English is unclear, please stop me and I’ll rephrase.”
claim_review_spans.R8: If they say yes, you get a speaking target. If they say no, you learn *why* (time, role expectations, rubric, confidence) and you can negotiate from there.
claim_review_spans.R9: It may have been about pronunciation—but it also could have been nervous laughter, not “mocking.” Either way, you don’t need to solve it emotionally right now. For the presentation, you only need to prevent the same failure mode:
claim_review_spans.R10: - **Don’t rely on spontaneous explanation.** Use a prepared “script” you can read closely.
claim_review_spans.R11: - **Use a speaking plan that matches your slides**, not your memory.
claim_review_spans.R12: For your part, make it **3 parts only**. Each part is 1–2 sentences, rehearsed *with your slides open*:
claim_review_spans.R13: 1. **What you did** (method)
claim_review_spans.R14: 2. **What changed / what you found** (result)
claim_review_spans.R15: 3. **Why it matters** (1 key takeaway)
claim_review_spans.R16: If you keep getting stuck, it’s usually because you’re trying to say too much. Reduce it until you can deliver it smoothly.
claim_review_spans.R17: - your slides’ slide titles (or just the slide text for your part), and
claim_review_spans.R18: - what your result difference was (one sentence in your own words)
claim_review_spans.R19: …and I can help you write a short speaking script you can rehearse.
claim_review_spans.R20: When they laughed / said “what?”, was it mainly because you **couldn’t find the words**, or because you **said something unclear about the method/result**?

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes sense that you’re uncomfortable. In your place, it’s not “rudeness” to want basic clarity and respect—you’re dealing with a mismatch between what you *assumed* “make yourself at home” meant and what your housemates are actually doing. And right now you’re hungry + stressed, so it’s totally reasonable that you want a low-conflict way to handle it.
claim_review_spans.R2: Also: you’re not necessarily “difficult.” Many cultures differ on sharing, but you still get to set boundaries—especially when it’s about *your food* and privacy.
claim_review_spans.R3: You need two things: (1) get food without conflict, (2) signal a boundary without a big argument.
claim_review_spans.R4: - If you have your own food upstairs: eat that.
claim_review_spans.R5: - If not, you can do a short “excuse” to get what you need:
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Script:** “Sorry—I haven’t eaten yet. I’m going to grab something from the fridge real quick.”
claim_review_spans.R7: This isn’t rude; it’s just letting them know you’re doing something normal.
claim_review_spans.R8: If they offer takeaway again, you can accept without accepting the “your food is shared” rule:
claim_review_spans.R9: Don’t try to do a deep explanation while friends are in the kitchen. Do it when it’s just you + housemates (or at least when it’s quieter).
claim_review_spans.R10: - “From now on I’ll label my stuff, and if you want any, just ask first, please.”
claim_review_spans.R11: This avoids blaming them for culture; it states your preference and creates a clear method.
claim_review_spans.R12: What you’re noticing (“make yourself at home” + then strangers using your things) is exactly why you need *a specific rule*, not a cultural guess. Boundaries can be:
claim_review_spans.R13: - “If you want to share, let’s agree on common food vs my personal stuff.”
claim_review_spans.R14: You actually don’t need to have already said “that’s my food” to deserve respect now. But it will make things easier to say it clearly once—then you won’t have to keep hiding upstairs.
claim_review_spans.R15: When they used your food, did you see *who* took it (or was it unclear), and are your housemates generally friendly when you speak normally with them?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful and scary—especially being new to university and still adjusting to studying in English. I can’t fully “know” what your professor meant from one mark, but I *can* help you separate what the feedback likely means from the bigger story your brain is telling you (“I’m not the kind of person who can do this”).
claim_review_spans.R2: “Needs your own argument” usually means **the paper isn’t only describing the readings**—it needs a clearer stance that you defend, with analysis and reasons (not just rewording sources).
claim_review_spans.R3: And importantly: **changing wording from readings doesn’t automatically prove you created your own argument.**
claim_review_spans.R4: It’s possible to write in your own sentences and still have the *structure/claim* be too close to the authors’ ideas.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Your thesis/central claim is unclear or too broad
claim_review_spans.R6: - You summarize instead of argue (no strong “so what?”)
claim_review_spans.R7: - You don’t take a position that could be challenged
claim_review_spans.R8: So: you’re not “wrong” about what you did, but you may need a different *kind* of thinking than you used at home.
claim_review_spans.R9: I hear how much you’re spiraling, and you want reassurance. Here’s the most honest version:
claim_review_spans.R10: - **A 48 on the first paper is not proof that you can’t succeed.**
claim_review_spans.R11: - It’s proof that **you have something specific to learn** (argument/thesis/analysis and probably structure/academic English).
claim_review_spans.R12: - Many first-year international students (and plenty of domestic students) do not nail “argument” on paper 1, even after working hard.
claim_review_spans.R13: One bad grade is a *signal*, not a life verdict.
claim_review_spans.R14: You’re overwhelmed, and the deadline confusion will make your brain freeze. You don’t need to drop the class yet—first you need to confirm what’s due and where.
claim_review_spans.R15: **One quick step (takes 2–3 minutes):**
claim_review_spans.R16: - In your learning platform, check for:
claim_review_spans.R17: - If you can, open **the “Assignments” list for each course** (not the single open page) and confirm which one says “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.”
claim_review_spans.R18: If you paste the assignment titles (just the titles + “tomorrow 5 p.m.” text), I can help you figure out which one it is.
claim_review_spans.R19: When sentences feel “wrong,” it’s often because you’re trying to write the final paper in your head before you’ve built anything. A helpful trick:
claim_review_spans.R20: **Write a messy version in bullets for 20 minutes.** No full sentences.
claim_review_spans.R21: 1) **Your claim** (1 sentence): “This paper argues that ____.”
claim_review_spans.R22: 2) **2–3 reasons** (bullets)
claim_review_spans.R23: 3) **For each reason, 1 piece of evidence** you’ll use (a quote or paraphrase note)
claim_review_spans.R24: Then you’re not stuck trying to produce perfect English immediately—you’re building the argument first.
claim_review_spans.R25: For the “tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page: **what is the assignment name/title shown there?** (Copy it exactly if you can.)

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really lonely and confusing—especially so early after arriving and when you *are* making an effort. I also hear a lot of pain in what you’re concluding (“they obviously don’t want me around,” “if I stop trying I won’t look desperate”). Two quick things can be true at once: (1) it’s possible those specific classmates were genuinely busy, and (2) you’re still getting strong signals of exclusion in the *way* you’ve experienced things.
claim_review_spans.R2: I wouldn’t say “there isn’t much point going to the club again” yet. Based on what you described, the bigger issue looks like **unclear invitations + you feeling like any attempt will expose you**, so you retreat before people have a chance to include you.
claim_review_spans.R3: - “Busy” two times = not necessarily rejection. People often avoid planning with new people even if they’re friendly, because it feels risky/awkward.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Talking about Saturday right next to you = they might assume you aren’t interested, or they forgot you need an explicit invite.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Memes from one person = that can be politeness *or* a small bridge—they’re at least comfortable interacting with you.
claim_review_spans.R6: None of this proves “they don’t want you around.” It proves you haven’t yet had a clear, low-pressure moment where someone includes you directly.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Step 1 (today/next club meeting): make a small, specific invitation**
claim_review_spans.R8: You can message or say something like:
claim_review_spans.R9: - “Hey, are you going to anything this Saturday? I’m free—want to join?”
claim_review_spans.R10: - “I’m going to get food after the meeting. Anyone wants to come?”
claim_review_spans.R11: Specific + low stakes = easier for people to say yes.
claim_review_spans.R12: **Step 2: don’t rely on group-chat guessing**
claim_review_spans.R13: Group chats often move fast and people may not read/notice everyone. Instead:
claim_review_spans.R14: - After sending a message, if it’s unread, follow up in person if you see someone.
claim_review_spans.R15: - Or reply directly to someone who *is* active in the chat: “You said you’re free on Saturday—what are you thinking?”
claim_review_spans.R16: **Step 3: go for a short time, but stay for one interaction**
claim_review_spans.R17: If staying only 10 minutes feels like “proving you tried,” you can make it more effective:
claim_review_spans.R18: - Go for the usual time (or 20–30 minutes),
claim_review_spans.R19: - Pick **one** person you’ll talk to for 2 minutes (not “make friends,” just talk).
claim_review_spans.R20: Unread messages aren’t automatically a social rejection. People can be busy, distracted, or forget to check chat.
claim_review_spans.R21: If you feel embarrassed, here’s a better tactic than stopping:
claim_review_spans.R22: - If no one answers, you still use the next meeting to approach one person directly.
claim_review_spans.R23: > “There isn’t much point going to the club again, right?”

claim_review_spans.R2: - Room payment due **Friday** (in **~4 days**).
claim_review_spans.R3: - You’ll have **$500** available; you only need **$200 more**.
claim_review_spans.R4: - You have **10 days left** in the sense of “last time they accepted late,” but it’s **still risky** to assume late will be OK without confirmation.
claim_review_spans.R5: - You’re considering cash shifts because they seem easier than school work paperwork—but you **haven’t started** and “no work permission needed” might be incorrect.
claim_review_spans.R6: Even if they let you pay late before, asking now reduces stress and protects you from last-minute refusal.
claim_review_spans.R7: > Hi [Name], I’m sorry for the situation—my family transfer was delayed this month. I can pay **$500 by Friday** as planned, and I will send the **remaining $200 on [day]** (via [method]). Could you confirm this arrangement works?
claim_review_spans.R8: If you only need $200, you can also offer an exact date: e.g., “by Wednesday” or “by next Monday.”
claim_review_spans.R9: - Ask your mum for a **small targeted amount** for the room (not the whole month).
claim_review_spans.R10: - If possible, ask a trusted friend/student to **advance $200** and you repay in a set number of days.
claim_review_spans.R11: I can’t confirm the “no permission needed” claim. In the US, many cash jobs for students still require authorization depending on visa type and how the work is structured. The safest move is:
claim_review_spans.R12: - Use your school’s **international student office / immigration advising** or a campus employment office to confirm what types of work you can do *on your exact status*.
claim_review_spans.R13: - In the meantime, do **non-work** options that don’t count as employment (e.g., short-term help that’s clearly not paid labor) only if that actually fits your situation.
claim_review_spans.R14: Since your need is time-sensitive ($200 before Friday), you may need to combine: **(A) payment arrangement** + **(B) small family/friend transfer**, and only then explore work properly.
claim_review_spans.R15: Even if someone says students don’t need permission, that can be wrong or incomplete—and if it’s wrong, it could create serious immigration risk later. Because your immediate problem is small ($200), I’d prioritize the payment arrangement + small transfer first, and only then handle employment paperwork/eligibility.
claim_review_spans.R16: What’s your **visa/immigration status** (or did you arrive on an F-1 student visa)?
claim_review_spans.R17: You can tell me just “F-1” or “not sure” — I don’t need any document numbers.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful—especially in a lab group where you *already* feel under pressure and then your message doesn’t come out the way you planned. And it makes sense your brain feels “tired” after speaking English all day; fatigue can hit hardest right when you need confidence and quick words.
claim_review_spans.R2: 1) **Their reaction doesn’t automatically mean you “can’t speak.”** People laugh for lots of reasons (awkwardness, surprise, not knowing what to say), and repeating “what?” can be about *clarity and speed* more than ability.
claim_review_spans.R3: 2) **Task assignment isn’t the same as the final grading decision.** Your teammates are giving you guesses (“same group mark” vs “speaking marked separately”). The truth will be whatever the rubric and instructor say.
claim_review_spans.R4: 3) **Practicing only three sentences can trap you.** If you freeze when you get stuck, you end up running the same rehearsed lines instead of building a flexible explanation.
claim_review_spans.R5: Ask for a quick check so you’re not deciding based on teammate assumptions.
claim_review_spans.R6: **Option A (best): email/message your TA/professor**
claim_review_spans.R7: Subject: Group presentation – speaking role / grading rubric question
claim_review_spans.R8: Our group presentation is coming up soon. I’m an international student and sometimes struggle with clarity when speaking quickly in English. I wanted to ask: **is there a speaking component that’s graded separately from the group content**, and is there a rubric I can review? Also, could you suggest what role would be best for me within the group (e.g., presenting one short section vs. voiceover vs. slides)?
claim_review_spans.R9: **Option B (if you already have the rubric link in a course page):** open it and paste the “presentation/speaking” part here (even a short excerpt). I can help you interpret it.
claim_review_spans.R10: Until you know the rubric, you can propose a role that protects you and still helps your team. For example:
claim_review_spans.R11: - **“Slides + short speaking blocks”**: you speak only during *your* slide(s), and your teammates cover transitions.
claim_review_spans.R12: - **Voiceover from a script** (readable script, not memory): you can keep it simple and natural.
claim_review_spans.R13: - **Q&A reserve**: you only answer 1–2 predictable questions you prepare.
claim_review_spans.R14: - **“Method/result narrator”**: 60–90 seconds total, then stop.
claim_review_spans.R15: If you want, I can help you craft exactly what to say to your teammates.
claim_review_spans.R16: Instead of repeating three sentences, practice a **simple pattern** you can fall back on even if words fail:
claim_review_spans.R17: For each slide, make it a 3-step micro-explanation:
claim_review_spans.R18: 1. **What this slide is** (“This slide shows…”)
claim_review_spans.R19: 2. **What happened / the key result** (“The main result is…”)
claim_review_spans.R20: 3. **So what** (“This suggests… / This means…”)
claim_review_spans.R21: - You’re allowed to look at the note.
claim_review_spans.R22: - You’re allowed to say “Let me rephrase” or “In other words…”
claim_review_spans.R23: Even one phrase like **“What this means is…”** can be your lifesaver when you blank.
claim_review_spans.R24: When is the presentation (roughly—today/tomorrow/this week), and do you have a rubric or instructions posted somewhere (even a screenshot/excerpt)?
claim_review_spans.R25: If you share the timeline and whatever you can find about how presentations are graded (or paste the rubric text), I’ll help you decide whether to ask for speaking time, negotiate a smaller speaking portion, or choose a slides-only role—and I’ll draft a message you can send.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really uncomfortable—especially because you already said “maybe,” and now it’s turned into people being in your shared space and using your food. Your feelings make sense, and you’re not “difficult” for wanting basic clarity and boundaries. What’s happening is mostly a communication mismatch: you were being polite, but you didn’t get to set the terms.
claim_review_spans.R2: Also: you *don’t* need to “accuse” anyone to protect your space. You just need simple, specific rules.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Get food that’s yours without entering the kitchen right now.** If you have any safe backup (snacks, instant food, bottled drink), use that.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **If you have to use the kitchen:** wait until there’s a lull and then go in with a neutral script (below). You don’t have to justify yourself—just do what you need.
claim_review_spans.R5: Your goal is to make it factual and low-drama: *“I need X.”* Here are a few ready-to-use lines.
claim_review_spans.R6: - “Hey—just a headspring for me. Could we keep visitors to **agreed times**? I’m still settling in.”
claim_review_spans.R7: - “I’m okay with visitors sometimes, but can we please **message me first** before friends come over?”
claim_review_spans.R8: This addresses the real issue (timing/permission) without discussing their culture.
claim_review_spans.R9: You can keep it very simple:
claim_review_spans.R10: - “By the way, that food is **mine**. Could you please not use my groceries?”
claim_review_spans.R11: - “I’m using my own groceries—can we keep them separate?”
claim_review_spans.R12: If you want even softer wording:
claim_review_spans.R13: - “I’m trying to keep my food for myself since I bought it for my meals.”
claim_review_spans.R14: - “I’m just about to eat—then I’ll go back to my room for a bit. No worries.”
claim_review_spans.R15: 1) Eat somehow (even if it’s just something quick).
claim_review_spans.R16: 2) In the moment, don’t explain a lot. Use a short line.
claim_review_spans.R17: **Soon (next time they’re calm, not during visitors):**
claim_review_spans.R18: - “I want to be clear about my food—please don’t use my groceries unless I say it’s okay. Also, for visitors, could we agree first so it’s not awkward for me?”
claim_review_spans.R19: That’s it. No long apology, no debate about culture.
claim_review_spans.R20: Right now, you’re acting like “they’ll understand the unstated rule.” You don’t need to guess anymore. In shared living situations, it’s normal to say clearly what you’re comfortable with—especially in the first weeks of settling in.
claim_review_spans.R21: 1) Are you sharing a **kitchen only**, or do you share other things too (bathroom, fridge shelf space, etc.)?

claim_review_spans.R1: I’m really sorry—getting a first paper back as a brand-new student can feel like the whole “I belong here” question gets decided in one number. That 48 is painful, especially when you already spent a lot of time. But based on what you shared, I don’t think this is a sign you “can’t do university in English.” It sounds much more like you’re hitting a normal transition problem: understanding what *your professor means by “your own argument”* and how to format that in a first-year assignment style.
claim_review_spans.R2: If you rewrote/paraphrased readings into your own sentences, that *is* your own writing. So your confusion is valid. What feedback like “needs your own argument” usually means something slightly different, like one (or more) of these:
claim_review_spans.R3: - You may have summarized sources but didn’t clearly state a specific stance (what you think) and prove it.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Your points may not have been organized around a clear claim (the “argument”), even if the sentences were your own.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Your paragraphs may have “supported information” but not connected back to a central thesis.
claim_review_spans.R6: - You might still be too close to the structure/wording of the reading (not plagiarizing necessarily—just not yet showing your *analysis*).
claim_review_spans.R7: So: the feedback is about **thinking/structure**, not your ability to write English or your worth as a student.
claim_review_spans.R8: Think of your first paper like a baseline. You’ve learned something concrete already:
claim_review_spans.R9: - and that you need a clearer thesis/argument structure.
claim_review_spans.R10: That’s fixable. Plenty of students get their first mark back before they fully understand the “game” of university writing. It’s not “you vs. English”—it’s learning the genre and expectations.
claim_review_spans.R11: Right now your brain is overloaded because you’re not sure which class/assignment is due. You don’t need more anxiety—you need one clear check.
claim_review_spans.R12: **Can you open the assignment page and tell me the exact class name/course code shown at the top of the page?**
claim_review_spans.R13: Once I know that, I can help you determine whether it’s the same class as the 48-mark paper or the other one, and what the next best step is.
claim_review_spans.R14: Dropping can be a sensible choice sometimes—but it should be based on information, not panic. Since you’re already thinking “another load of questions would make my head worse,” I suggest a *tiny* decision-step:
claim_review_spans.R15: **Do not decide to drop yet.** Take one step that gives you information within 20–30 minutes:
claim_review_spans.R16: 1) confirm which course has “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.”
claim_review_spans.R17: 2) skim the assignment prompt for that course and identify: **(a) thesis/argument requirement** and **(b) format/length**.
claim_review_spans.R18: Then you’ll be deciding with facts, not fear.
claim_review_spans.R19: From what you wrote: you are not wrong to feel hurt, but you *are* wrong to conclude “I’m not the kind of person who can do university in English” based on one grade and one piece of feedback. The “own argument” comment is normal and teachable.
claim_review_spans.R20: Reply with the **course name/code** shown on the “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page, and I’ll help you figure out what you should do next (and how to start writing without everything feeling “wrong”).

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful and confusing—especially being new to the U.S. and not having anyone yet. From what you wrote, I don’t think there’s enough evidence to conclude “they obviously don’t want me around.” What you *do* have is a pattern of “I tried to connect and it didn’t land,” and that pattern is making you feel like you’ll be judged as desperate if you keep trying.
claim_review_spans.R2: Also, your classmates’ behavior can mean lots of non-personal things:
claim_review_spans.R3: - Some people are awkward with new students and don’t know how to include you yet.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Group talk next to you often means they assume you’ll join, but they don’t think to *turn toward you* and directly invite.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Unread messages in a group chat don’t necessarily mean rejection; it can mean people check at different times, or they don’t want to reply while they’re in the middle of plans.
claim_review_spans.R6: I wouldn’t jump to that conclusion yet. Quitting after a couple of moments is understandable emotionally, but it risks making the situation worse for you—because the only way to get included is for you to stay in the environment long enough to be recognized as “a regular person,” not a one-time interaction.
claim_review_spans.R7: A better goal than “be friends immediately” is: **get 1 low-pressure connection**.
claim_review_spans.R8: > “Hi, I’m new here—do you want to get coffee before the next meeting? It can be quick.”
claim_review_spans.R9: > “Hey, when you were talking about Saturday—was that a club plan or personal plans? I’m still learning how things work here.”
claim_review_spans.R10: **Why this helps:** it gives them a simple choice and reduces the “are you trying to join something?” discomfort.
claim_review_spans.R11: Instead of stopping messages (which protects your pride but prevents connection), do this once:
claim_review_spans.R12: > “Hi everyone—are we doing anything for Saturday? I’m new and would love to join if it’s open.”
claim_review_spans.R13: If they still don’t respond after that, then you have more real information—and you can switch to asking one person directly (instead of relying on the group chat).
claim_review_spans.R14: At the club gathering, did you already introduce yourself (name + “new student”) to anyone, or did you mostly stand nearby and listen?
claim_review_spans.R15: If you tell me that, I’ll suggest the best “next attempt” script for your exact situation and how often to try without overexposing yourself.

claim_review_spans.R1: Hey—thanks for telling me. I don’t think you’re “bad at this.” This is a very normal first-semester problem: your cash flow got squeezed (your mom sent less), and now there’s a clear deadline (Friday). The key is to handle the $200 shortfall *quickly* and in a way that doesn’t put your status at risk.
claim_review_spans.R2: - Next room payment: **$800 total**
claim_review_spans.R3: - You currently have about **$500 left** for the payment
claim_review_spans.R4: - So you need **$200 by Friday**
claim_review_spans.R5: - Room provider allows late payment before (but you’re assuming)
claim_review_spans.R6: Even if they let you be late last time, don’t assume—ask clearly. It also prevents them from marking you as “missed payment” if they have rules.
claim_review_spans.R7: > Hi [Name], I’m writing about the room payment due this Friday. I’m short by about $200 due to a delay with my funds from home. I can pay the remaining **$200 on [day/time]**, and I will submit the full amount by **[your guaranteed date]**. Is it okay to pay this way / can you allow a late partial payment? Thank you.
claim_review_spans.R8: If you want, tell me what you can realistically pay by **Wednesday** (or whatever day you choose), and I’ll help you phrase the dates cleanly.
claim_review_spans.R9: I get why that sounds tempting—fewer forms, faster money. But I can’t safely agree with “students don’t need work permission.” In the U.S., whether work is allowed depends on your **immigration/visa status**, and many “cash shifts” can create serious risk (ex: being treated as unauthorized work).
claim_review_spans.R10: - either ask your school’s international student office what kinds of work are allowed **for your status**, or
claim_review_spans.R11: - use other options first to cover this **one payment**.
claim_review_spans.R12: Pick 1–2 options; don’t rely on all of them:
claim_review_spans.R13: 1) **Ask your mom for a small extra transfer**
claim_review_spans.R14: Even if she sent less this month, you can explain: “Room payment is due Friday; I’m short $200.”
claim_review_spans.R15: 2) **Ask a trusted friend/classmate for a small temporary loan** (with a clear repayment date)
claim_review_spans.R16: This is common when you’re new and cashflow is tight. You can even write a short agreement via message: amount + repayment date.
claim_review_spans.R17: 3) **Small campus income that’s clearly permitted**
claim_review_spans.R18: If your university offers on-campus jobs, those are usually the “right channel” (but we need your status/work authorization to be sure). For this week, even **on-campus help** or approved work can be safer than cash-only arrangements.
claim_review_spans.R19: 4) **Ask housing for a short extension / installment**
claim_review_spans.R20: You can frame it as: partial payment Friday, rest by a specific date.
claim_review_spans.R21: Do you know what your **visa/status** is (even roughly), or have you already met with your university’s **international student office** since arriving?
claim_review_spans.R22: If you don’t know, no problem—just tell me whether you have an appointment/meeting scheduled with them, or when your campus orientation ended.
claim_review_spans.R23: Also: what day/time do you think you could realistically come up with the extra $200 (Thursday? Wednesday night? Thursday morning)?

claim_review_spans.R3: - The laughter likely felt personal, but laughter in group settings is often messy/awkward (people sometimes laugh at misunderstanding, stress, or the tension of communication—not necessarily at your value). Still, it’s valid that it hurt.
claim_review_spans.R4: - You’re getting mixed messages about how group work is marked. That means the **rubric/assessment method** matters a lot before you decide what to do.
claim_review_spans.R5: Don’t ask “Can I speak?” (too broad, invites a yes/no and more anxiety). Instead, ask for a **small speaking commitment** tied to a specific part.
claim_review_spans.R6: You can do this in a quick message to the teammate who seems most involved, or to the lab leader/TA if you have that contact.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Option A: message a teammate (short)**
claim_review_spans.R8: > “Hi—quick question about the presentation grading. Is speaking a separate portion or is it part of the group mark? I want to understand the expectations so I can prepare correctly.”
claim_review_spans.R9: > “I’m practicing the explanation, but I get stuck when presenting. Would it be possible for me to speak for a small section (like explaining what I did / one slide) and keep the rest slide-only?”
claim_review_spans.R10: If you tell me **who you can contact** (lab leader/TA vs teammate) and whether you have the presentation title/topic, I can tailor the exact wording.
claim_review_spans.R11: Given what you wrote, I’d recommend you **ask for a speaking part**, but **make it small and specific**. Reason: you’re already practicing, and you don’t want this moment to accidentally become a long-term pattern (“quiet student = no speaking”).
claim_review_spans.R12: - You prepare the slides (you’re already doing that),
claim_review_spans.R13: - and you speak **only the 1–2 key sentences** on *one* slide (or the “what I did” part).
claim_review_spans.R14: That reduces risk and makes it measurable: if your team sees you can deliver a small section, they may be more willing to expand later.
claim_review_spans.R15: Until you know the grading:
claim_review_spans.R16: - treat “same group mark” as possible too,
claim_review_spans.R17: - but don’t guess based on a teammate’s comment.
claim_review_spans.R18: So the best use of energy is: **clarify assessment → then choose your strategy**.
claim_review_spans.R19: You mentioned you keep repeating the same three sentences. A lot of non-native speakers get stuck because they memorize lines, then lose their place.
claim_review_spans.R20: - Slide title (1 word cue)
claim_review_spans.R21: - 3 bullet keywords (e.g., “method / control / result”)
claim_review_spans.R22: 1) “For this step, we used ___.”
claim_review_spans.R23: 2) “The key result was ___.”
claim_review_spans.R24: You can still sound natural without memorizing exact wording.
claim_review_spans.R25: If you want, paste the **three sentences you’ve been practising** (even rough English is fine), and I’ll help you rewrite them into a clearer, easier-to-deliver structure for your slides.
claim_review_spans.R26: “Maybe being quiet is just my place” is a painful thought. But you’re not “quiet by nature”—you’re **in a high-pressure communication situation in a second-language environment**. That’s normal to struggle with at first. You deserve a role that matches what you can contribute—not a role others choose for you because it’s easier.
claim_review_spans.R27: **Quick question (just one):** Who do you think you can contact first—your **lab TA/lab instructor/mentor**, or mainly your **teammates**?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really stressful—especially when you’re new, trying to be polite in a different culture, and at the same time your boundaries are getting crossed. And just to validate: it’s *completely normal* to be unsure about what “make yourself at home” means. In your position, you’re not automatically “difficult”—you’re trying to communicate clearly when you don’t yet share the same expectations.
claim_review_spans.R2: Even if a household culture is “sharing,” it still needs basic clarity: **“shared food vs. my food”** and **“visitors in shared spaces”**. You can handle this without sounding aggressive.
claim_review_spans.R3: **“I’m hungry—does anyone have something I can eat quickly?”**
claim_review_spans.R4: This avoids going into the kitchen while they’re there and also keeps it neutral.
claim_review_spans.R5: - If you have anything sealed (snack, instant food, takeaway voucher, etc.), use that for now. Then you deal with the communication when they’re calmer.
claim_review_spans.R6: **Option C (if you can’t eat): ask for a quick time**
claim_review_spans.R7: **“Sorry—just today I’m tired and I need quiet. Can you let me use the kitchen after your friends leave?”**
claim_review_spans.R8: You need to set two boundaries gently:
claim_review_spans.R9: 1) **Visitors:** whether guests are allowed and when
claim_review_spans.R10: 2) **Personal items/food:** what is yours, and what you’re okay sharing
claim_review_spans.R11: - **“Hey, just so I understand—are friends okay in the kitchen like this? I’m a bit unsure about the routine here.”**
claim_review_spans.R12: - **“Could you ask me first next time? I’m still adjusting and I need to plan.”**
claim_review_spans.R13: - **“Thank you, but I actually bought that food for myself—could you check with me next time before using my stuff?”**
claim_review_spans.R14: - **“I’m not finished—would you mind keeping my items separate?”**
claim_review_spans.R15: If you worry it will seem “weird,” remember: you’re not accusing anyone—you’re just setting a new rule you didn’t know existed.
claim_review_spans.R16: You can address the food without drama, even without accusing anyone:
claim_review_spans.R17: > **“I’m still learning the household rules here. For my part, I don’t mind sharing in general, but I need a clear line between shared items and my personal food.”**
claim_review_spans.R18: When you say “make yourself at home,” do they also seem to share *their own* food freely (e.g., “help yourself” with groceries), or is it mostly that they assume your things are shared too?
claim_review_spans.R19: Reply with just: **“they share theirs a lot”** or **“it feels like they assume my things”**—and I’ll help you choose the best exact wording for the next conversation.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful and scary—especially being only a few weeks in, in a new language, and already getting a mark that feels like a verdict on *you*. I can’t tell you that you’re “not wrong” about dropping it, because I don’t yet know what the assignment was really testing or what the class expectations are. But I *can* say this:
claim_review_spans.R2: It usually means the marker thinks you didn’t clearly do one specific academic skill yet—most commonly:
claim_review_spans.R3: - you summarized sources instead of taking a clear stance,
claim_review_spans.R4: - your “argument” wasn’t explicit (or didn’t stay consistent),
claim_review_spans.R5: - your points weren’t organized to prove a thesis.
claim_review_spans.R6: Also, “needs your own argument” often appears when a student has used sources/changed wording, but the *structure of thinking* isn’t yet “yours” in the way the rubric means. This is super common for first-year international students, even when the writing is genuinely their own.
claim_review_spans.R7: You can absolutely write in your own words and still be missing what the grader means by “your own argument.” For example, you might have:
claim_review_spans.R8: - but still not made a clear claim like: *“I argue that X because of A and B, and here’s how each source supports my claim.”*
claim_review_spans.R9: So your wording may be original, while your *argument* is still too close to the readings or too indirect.
claim_review_spans.R10: This part is a very concrete problem, not a “you can’t do it” problem. Confusion here can happen easily when you’re new and juggling multiple class sites.
claim_review_spans.R11: 1) On your assignment page, look for the **course code / course title** and the **assignment name** (even if you have to copy it here).
claim_review_spans.R12: 2) Then check whether the “due tomorrow 5 p.m.” page shows:
claim_review_spans.R13: - the same class as the paper that got 48, or
claim_review_spans.R14: If you paste the **course title/code** and **assignment name** from that “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page (you can remove anything personal), I’ll help you confirm which class it belongs to and what to do first.
claim_review_spans.R15: I hear that dropping feels “sensible.” That feeling makes sense when you’re overwhelmed. But dropping is usually an irreversible response to something that might be fixable with one targeted improvement.
claim_review_spans.R16: A compromise that protects you without committing to dropping immediately is:
claim_review_spans.R17: - **Contact the instructor/TA** with one specific question about how they want “your own argument” shown.
claim_review_spans.R18: - After you get another piece of feedback (or even a quick clarification), you can decide again.
claim_review_spans.R19: You spent nearly all week on the first paper. That means you *do* belong in university-level work—you were putting in real effort. Right now your brain is interpreting feedback as identity (“I’m not the kind of person who can do this”), but feedback is about a specific performance for a specific assignment.
claim_review_spans.R20: What exactly does the rubric/feedback say besides “needs your own argument”? Even 1–2 short lines (or the wording of the criteria) would help me translate what they likely mean into a clear plan for your next paper.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really lonely—especially because it happened right after you arrived, and you’re trying to do the “right” things (inviting lunch, showing up to club events) but it doesn’t feel like you’re getting a clear opening back.
claim_review_spans.R2: A few things that might be going on (none of this means you’re “unwanted”):
claim_review_spans.R3: - **“Busy” is not always “no.”** People often default to busy when they’re awkward, distracted, or don’t know you well yet.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **The club planning thing sounds ambiguous, not hostile.** If they were talking right beside you, they may have assumed you didn’t need the info, or they just forgot to include you in the moment.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **Unread group chat messages can become a self-fulfilling spiral.** Not because you’re wrong to feel awkward—but because once you start believing “they don’t want me here,” it becomes harder to read what’s actually happening.
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Memes = partial connection.** Even if it’s “polite,” it’s still a real bridge. Polite can turn into friendly if you give it structure.
claim_review_spans.R7: So to your question—**no, I wouldn’t say there’s “no point” going to the club again.** I’d call it a “wrong strategy, not wrong person” situation. The missing piece is usually *how* you approach and *what kind* of invitation you make, not whether you should try.
claim_review_spans.R8: **Goal:** make it easy for people to include you without putting you in the position of “waiting to be noticed.”
claim_review_spans.R9: 1) **Go once more, and choose one concrete role**
claim_review_spans.R10: - People are more likely to respond to *tasks* and *time-based plans* than to a vague social invitation.
claim_review_spans.R11: 2) **Use a “specific yes/no” invite (instead of lunch + open-ended)**
claim_review_spans.R12: - “Hey, I’m going to get food after this—want to join?”
claim_review_spans.R13: - “What are you doing Saturday? I’m free in the afternoon; want to join me?”
claim_review_spans.R14: 3) **If you posted in the group chat, follow up with a short message that includes you in the plan**
claim_review_spans.R15: - “Hi everyone—I'm new here and still figuring out Saturday. Is anyone going to the club activity / doing something fun? If so, I’d love to join.”
claim_review_spans.R16: 4) **Don’t interpret “not invited directly” as rejection**
claim_review_spans.R17: - Instead interpret it as: *you haven’t created a clear invitation channel yet.*
claim_review_spans.R18: You can send something like:
claim_review_spans.R19: - “Hey! I’m trying to make plans for Saturday—anyone want to go together? Totally okay if not.”

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really stressful—especially because it’s only been a few weeks, and the money gap is immediate (due Friday). And no: asking for help or feeling worried doesn’t mean you’re “bad at this.” First-year + language adjustment + new routines can make money problems feel 10x bigger.
claim_review_spans.R2: Let’s focus on the **one concrete deadline**: **your remaining $200 due Friday**.
claim_review_spans.R3: Even if you think you can pay late, don’t assume it—messages can change.
claim_review_spans.R4: Reply to your housing person with something simple like:
claim_review_spans.R5: > “Hi, I’m confirming the remaining balance due this Friday is **$200**. Can I pay late if needed, and if so, what date/time should I send it? I’m arranging the transfer now.”
claim_review_spans.R6: This does two things: it reduces risk, and it buys you clarity fast.
claim_review_spans.R7: Because you only need **$200**, you don’t necessarily need a whole job—small bridging works.
claim_review_spans.R8: 1) **Ask your mom for a specific top-up** (small amount + clear reason)
claim_review_spans.R9: - Message: *“My room payment is due this Friday. I’m short by $200. Can you send $200 today/this week? I can repay you next month once my budget catches up.”*
claim_review_spans.R10: - If you’re worried she’ll be angry: emphasize it’s a **one-time gap** and **you have food/bus covered** already.
claim_review_spans.R11: 2) **Borrow from someone you trust (short-term, with a date)**
claim_review_spans.R12: - Script: *“I only need $200 by Friday for my room payment. I can repay on [date] when my next allowance arrives. Can you help as a short loan?”*
claim_review_spans.R13: 3) **Use fast “swap money” moves**
claim_review_spans.R14: - Sell something small (textbooks, electronics, furniture you don’t need).
claim_review_spans.R15: I can’t confirm the claim that “students don’t need work permission” for cash shifts in the U.S. Many students *do* need authorization for paid work, even if it’s cash. Doing unapproved work can create serious problems later (visa/status risk, reporting issues, institutional consequences).
claim_review_spans.R16: So I’d treat that option as **high-risk unless you verify your exact eligibility with your school’s international student office**.
claim_review_spans.R17: Who to email/ask (name may vary at your school):
claim_review_spans.R18: If you want, I can draft a short email that doesn’t overshare.
claim_review_spans.R19: 1) When you say “room payment is **800**,” is that **$800 total**, or is it **$800 next payment with $200 remaining** after you already set aside $600?
claim_review_spans.R20: 2) Do you have **any** other support options right now—like a friend who could loan $200, or your mom who can send a small transfer by this week?
claim_review_spans.R21: If you answer those, I’ll help you pick the fastest route and write the exact message(s) to send today.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful—especially in a lab group where you *need* to contribute clearly. And it also sounds like you’re not actually failing at the work; you’re getting hit by the two hardest things at once: (1) English pressure in real time and (2) feeling judged when you couldn’t explain yourself.
claim_review_spans.R2: - **Your accent/language can be the trigger, but it doesn’t automatically mean you “can’t speak.”** In early group work, people often react awkwardly when someone struggles—then it becomes a social moment. That doesn’t equal your ability.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Getting put next to “preparing slides” doesn’t have to be permanent.** It may reflect a safe default for them, or it may be how the group handled the last meeting. You can renegotiate before the presentation.
claim_review_spans.R4: For this presentation, you can aim for **a speaking role that is small, prepared, and low-risk**, rather than “perfect speaking” or “no speaking.”
claim_review_spans.R5: - **You speak for 30–60 seconds** (or one slide / one section), using **a script you can read from**
claim_review_spans.R6: - You don’t improvise. You practice *reading + delivery*.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Step 1 (now, 20 minutes):** Decide the smallest speaking role that still feels like “mine.”
claim_review_spans.R8: - “I will explain Slide 3 (the result difference) in ~45 seconds.”
claim_review_spans.R9: - “I will say the conclusion + one key number from my result.”
claim_review_spans.R10: - “I will read the methods step for my part of the lab.”
claim_review_spans.R11: **Step 2 (next 30–60 minutes):** Write a script that’s *not 3 sentences stuck in your head*.
claim_review_spans.R12: Use 5–7 short lines. Example template (customize to your slides):
claim_review_spans.R13: > “In my experiment, the results were different because of [reason].
claim_review_spans.R14: > Step [X] affects [variable].
claim_review_spans.R15: > The expected value was [X], but we observed [Y].
claim_review_spans.R16: > This leads to the interpretation that [main meaning].
claim_review_spans.R17: > In conclusion, the difference comes from [one phrase].”
claim_review_spans.R18: - reading it aloud slowly 5 times,
claim_review_spans.R19: - then once with a timer (even if you don’t hit perfect timing yet).
claim_review_spans.R20: **Step 3 (before the presentation):** Ask for the speaking part in a low-pressure way.
claim_review_spans.R21: You don’t need a debate about the rubric. You can frame it as helping the team run smoothly.
claim_review_spans.R22: You can say something like:
claim_review_spans.R23: > “I want to contribute to the speaking part. For the presentation, could I speak for just my section—like explaining Slide [X]—about one minute? I’ll have a script.”
claim_review_spans.R24: If they say “everyone gets the same mark,” you can respond:
claim_review_spans.R25: > “Great—then I’ll take my one-minute part so everyone hears the result clearly.”
claim_review_spans.R26: If they say speaking is separate:
claim_review_spans.R27: > “Then I want to do my best for my portion. I can speak from the slide notes so it’s clear.”
claim_review_spans.R28: Given what happened yesterday, I’d recommend **a speaking role that is small and scripted**—not because you “must prove yourself,” but because:
claim_review_spans.R29: - speaking practice under real conditions is how you’ll build confidence,
claim_review_spans.R30: - and your group is already labeling you as “non-speaker” based on one difficult moment.
claim_review_spans.R31: You can start small so you don’t feel exposed, while still changing the pattern.
claim_review_spans.R32: Even if their laughter was about your accent, it still doesn’t automatically mean they’ll be fair or supportive about your contributions. Their behavior was unkind/awkward. You’re allowed to take control of how you participate.
claim_review_spans.R33: 1) What is your presentation section—**what do you need to explain** (methods, the “result difference,” analysis, or conclusion)?
claim_review_spans.R34: 2) About how long is your part supposed to be—**30 seconds, 1 minute, or 3+ minutes**?
claim_review_spans.R35: If you paste the slide title(s) or the exact “result difference” sentence you’re trying to say, I can help you turn it into a short, easy-to-deliver script.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes a lot of sense that you feel stuck. You tried to be polite the way you were taught, but because you said “yeah maybe” (without clarifying), your housemates treated your answer as permission. Now the real problem isn’t just the visitors—it’s that you didn’t get to set clear boundaries *and* you’re dealing with hunger at the same time.
claim_review_spans.R2: A gentle truth: there’s no single “correct culture.” In shared living, “make yourself at home” usually means *“we’re friendly”*—but it still should come with clarity about what is shared vs. private. What you’re experiencing is common for international students: you’re being respectful, but your needs weren’t communicated.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1) **Text/call a housemate quietly (or speak to one person, not the group):**
claim_review_spans.R4: “Sorry—I'm hungry and I need to eat before things get busy. Are you using the kitchen right now? I’m going to get my food from the fridge/pantry.”
claim_review_spans.R5: 2) **Go get your own food quickly, even if they’re there:**
claim_review_spans.R6: If your food is identifiable, bring it out with you and eat at a different place in the house (your room, desk area). This signals “this is mine” without a big conversation.
claim_review_spans.R7: If you want, tell me: do you have *some* identifiable food (your name on it / a specific shelf / container), or is it mixed in communal areas? That changes what wording is safest.
claim_review_spans.R8: Your goal is: **clear future rules + explain your perspective briefly + ask what they prefer.**
claim_review_spans.R9: You can say something like:
claim_review_spans.R10: > “I want to check something—my food was in my place, so I was surprised it got used. In the future, can we keep personal food separate? If people want food, they can ask me first.”
claim_review_spans.R11: > “I’m okay with sharing in some situations, but I need to be clear about personal items. Next time, could you ask before using my food?”
claim_review_spans.R12: **Option C (if you don’t want to mention “my food” directly):**
claim_review_spans.R13: > “I’m still adjusting to house rules. For food, should we treat it as shared by default, or is personal food private? I’m a bit confused.”
claim_review_spans.R14: Notice: you’re not accusing anyone of “being wrong.” You’re setting a rule going forward.
claim_review_spans.R15: No—you don’t have to be “rude.” You just need *neutral clarity*. For next time, instead of “yeah maybe,” you can use language that protects you:
claim_review_spans.R16: - “**I’m not sure yet—ask me later.**”
claim_review_spans.R17: - “**I’m not comfortable with visitors in the kitchen—can we do it at a different time?**”
claim_review_spans.R18: - “**Let me check first, I’m keeping things private today.**”

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds *really* painful—especially because it’s your first semester abroad, your first time writing in English in a university setting, and you already invested a lot of time. I can see why a 48 would keep replaying in your head.
claim_review_spans.R2: But I don’t want to agree with the part that “one bad mark means you’re not the kind of person who can do university.” That conclusion is coming from fear, not evidence.
claim_review_spans.R3: This specific wording usually does **not** mean “you didn’t write your own words.” It more often means something like:
claim_review_spans.R4: - or your paragraphs stayed too close to the sources (summarizing) without turning that into your own claim,
claim_review_spans.R5: - or you didn’t explain *why* your evidence supports your claim,
claim_review_spans.R6: Also, rewriting from readings can still be “your writing” linguistically—professors may still feel the *thinking* is not yet yours in the way they need. That’s fixable.
claim_review_spans.R7: It makes sense you feel frozen when the deadline is “tomorrow at 5 p.m.” and you’re not sure which course it belongs to. When your brain is already stressed, details like “which class?” feel like they can break you.
claim_review_spans.R8: Open your course management system (Canvas / Blackboard / whatever you use) and do this for **the assignment page that says “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.”**:
claim_review_spans.R9: 1. Click the assignment title (or assignment details) and look for the **course name/code** displayed at the top.
claim_review_spans.R10: 2. Also check whether there’s a **due date/time zone** shown there.
claim_review_spans.R11: 3. If you can’t immediately find it, look at your **To-Do / Calendar** for tomorrow—does it list which class the submission is for?
claim_review_spans.R12: If you tell me the **exact course name/code** shown on that assignment page (just that text), I can help you figure out the fastest way to proceed.
claim_review_spans.R13: Dropping can be a sensible option sometimes—but right now it sounds like you’re considering it from a place of overload and shame (“my head is worse,” “I’m not that kind of person”). That’s not the same as making a calm choice based on workload, grades, and support.
claim_review_spans.R14: So instead of deciding “drop vs don’t drop” today, I’d suggest a *trial approach*:
claim_review_spans.R15: - get the deadline sorted,
claim_review_spans.R16: - then decide after you see what you can do with help/feedback.
claim_review_spans.R17: You are not wrong to take feedback seriously. But you *are* probably jumping to an extreme meaning from it. Many first-year students—especially when English is not their first language—get early marks that look scary while their underlying academic skills are still developing. This is exactly the stage where feedback is meant to teach you how the system expects arguments.
claim_review_spans.R18: 1) What subject/class is the one with the 48 (or what does the feedback document title say)?
claim_review_spans.R19: 2) On the “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page, what course name/code do you see at the top?
claim_review_spans.R20: If you answer those, we’ll tackle the deadline first and then I’ll help you turn “needs your own argument” into something you can actually do in your next paper.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes total sense that you feel discouraged. From your side, it’s not just “making friends takes time”—it’s *two direct lunch rejections*, plus standing near conversations where it’s unclear whether you’re being included, plus your club messages not getting replies. That combination can make you feel like you’re being avoided, even if other explanations are possible.
claim_review_spans.R2: I can’t know their motives, but I do think your conclusion (“there isn’t much point going to the club again”) is stronger than the evidence you actually have.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **They’re genuinely busy / distracted** that day (busy schedules are common in the first semester).
claim_review_spans.R4: - **You may be reading “private plans” risk onto everything**—they might have been talking about what the club is doing Saturday, but you couldn’t read the cues.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **Group dynamics:** sometimes people assume “someone else will invite,” especially in mixed groups. Not inviting you directly doesn’t automatically mean “we don’t want you around.”
claim_review_spans.R6: - **The meme person:** sending memes can be real connection, not just politeness—but even politeness is still engagement. It suggests they notice you.
claim_review_spans.R7: And also: **unread messages doesn’t necessarily mean rejection.** Group chat messages often get ignored because people are multitasking, in class, asleep, or they’re waiting to respond in the moment they’re free.
claim_review_spans.R8: If you go to the club and keep trying in a *slightly different way*, you’re not “desperate”; you’re doing the normal work of socializing. The difference is: instead of messages that might get overlooked, you switch to a **low-pressure, specific ask** in the moment.
claim_review_spans.R9: 1) **Fast inclusion move**
claim_review_spans.R10: > “Hi, I’m new here—what are you guys planning to do on Saturday? Is it connected to the club?”
claim_review_spans.R11: 2) **Direct but low-stakes invite**
claim_review_spans.R12: > “I’m going to grab food after this—want to join? If not, no worries.”
claim_review_spans.R13: 3) **Follow-up without sounding demanding**
claim_review_spans.R14: > “Sorry I missed the plan—should I come to the next meeting or is Saturday something separate?”
claim_review_spans.R15: These remove the ambiguity you mentioned (whether Saturday is club activity or private plans). People find it easier to respond to something *specific*.
claim_review_spans.R16: I’d say **don’t stop yet**—at least not based only on two lunch “busy” answers and unread messages.
claim_review_spans.R17: - If that second attempt clearly results in consistent dismissal or rudeness (not just “busy”), then you reassess and choose another way to meet people (another club, study group, dorm event, language exchange, etc.).
claim_review_spans.R18: You said: “If I stop trying, at least I won’t look desperate.”
claim_review_spans.R19: But in practice, the “desperate” risk is usually *in how you pressure people*, not in how often you reach out. Asking one clear, friendly question is normal—especially for a newcomer.
claim_review_spans.R20: When you sent messages in the club group chat, did you ask something *specific* (e.g., “What time are we meeting Saturday?”) or was it more general (“Anyone going?” / “Hi”)?

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes sense that this feels embarrassing, especially while you’re still settling into a new country. But a shortfall doesn’t mean you’re bad with money. You’ve already protected money for food and transport, and you’re addressing the payment before it’s due.
claim_review_spans.R2: **Two important corrections so you can plan accurately:**
claim_review_spans.R4: - If today is Monday and payment is due this Friday, you have **four days**, not ten.
claim_review_spans.R5: Being allowed to pay late last time doesn’t automatically mean it’s allowed again. You can send:
claim_review_spans.R6: > Hi [name], thanks for the reminder about the $800 room payment due this Friday. I can pay $500 by Friday, but I’m currently $300 short. Could we arrange for me to pay the $500 on Friday and the remaining $300 afterward? Please let me know whether this is possible, what deadline you could allow, and whether any late fee would apply.
claim_review_spans.R7: Only promise a date for the remaining $300 once you know it’s realistic. Keep their reply in writing, and check your housing agreement for late-payment terms.
claim_review_spans.R8: Today, ask your university’s student support office or international student office:
claim_review_spans.R9: > I’m facing a $300 housing-payment shortfall due this Friday. Are there emergency grants, short-term loans, or housing-support options available to international undergraduates? How quickly could assistance be provided?
claim_review_spans.R10: I can’t verify your university’s programs or your eligibility, so ask specifically about both eligibility and timing.
claim_review_spans.R11: If it feels safe to tell your mum, a factual message could be:
claim_review_spans.R12: > I haven’t clearly explained my housing costs: my next room payment is $800. After keeping money for food and transport, I have $500 available, so I’m $300 short for Friday. Is any extra help possible? If not, I need to know so I can arrange another option.
claim_review_spans.R13: **Being paid in cash does not remove work-authorization requirements.** Whether you can take that job depends on your immigration status and the work involved. Verify with your university’s international student adviser before accepting or starting any shifts. You haven’t started, so there’s still time to check first.
claim_review_spans.R14: For now, the most useful first action is sending the payment-arrangement message. **Does your room agreement say anything about late payments or fees?** You can share just that section with personal details removed.

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day while you’re still settling in can be exhausting. Then getting stuck, hearing laughter, and seeing your name assigned only to slides would understandably leave you feeling embarrassed and excluded. **You don’t have to accept “the quiet one” as your place in the group.** Struggling to explain a result in the moment is not the same as not understanding the lab.
claim_review_spans.R2: A few things are still uncertain: what they were laughing about, why they assigned you slides, and how speaking is graded. Your concern about your accent being the joke deserves to be taken seriously—but those events don’t yet prove that the group has decided you cannot speak.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **Check the grading requirements before spending more time rehearsing.** Look for the presentation rubric or assignment instructions on the course website. If you can’t find them, ask the instructor or teaching assistant:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Could you clarify whether the presentation has an individual speaking grade or only a group grade, and whether every member needs to speak? Our group has different understandings of the requirements.”
claim_review_spans.R5: 2. **Make your preference clear rather than treating the task list as final.** If you want to try a speaking part, you could send:
claim_review_spans.R6: > “I saw that I’m assigned to prepare the slides. I’d also like a short speaking section explaining my result. Can we agree on that and do one practice run together? When I pause, please give me a moment to finish.”
claim_review_spans.R7: A brief, defined section lets you participate without committing to a long explanation. If you prefer slides this time, that can also be a choice—once you know the grading consequences—not a verdict on your ability.
claim_review_spans.R8: 3. **Change the practice method, rather than repeating the same three sentences.** Take a short break first. Then use three prompts instead of a memorized paragraph:
claim_review_spans.R9: - “One possible reason is ___.” *(Only if supported by your lab work.)*
claim_review_spans.R10: If laughter or dismissive comments happen again, note the specific words and actions; you can raise those with the instructor or TA rather than having to prove someone’s intentions.
claim_review_spans.R11: **How soon is the presentation, and can you paste the grading section of the instructions, with personal details removed?**

claim_review_spans.R1: It sounds uncomfortable to feel like you need to stay upstairs in your own home—especially when you’re hungry. Wanting your food left alone and some say about visitors doesn’t make you difficult.
claim_review_spans.R2: There may be a communication mismatch here, but it’s too early to conclude that people here don’t care about others’ belongings. Your housemates might have heard “yeah maybe” as permission, and “I haven’t eaten yet” as a request for food rather than a concern about yours being used. That doesn’t make using your food okay; it means they may not yet understand what’s bothering you.
claim_review_spans.R3: **For right now, you don’t have to resolve everything before eating.** You can go downstairs just to prepare food, without staying to socialize:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Hey, I’m just going to make myself something to eat.”
claim_review_spans.R5: If walking into the group feels too uncomfortable, text a housemate:
claim_review_spans.R6: > “Hey, I haven’t eaten and I’m feeling awkward coming down with everyone there. I’m going to come make some food—could you make sure there’s space for me in the kitchen?”
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I noticed some food I bought for myself has been used. I hadn’t explained that I was keeping it for my own meals. Going forward, please ask before using my food. Could we agree on what’s shared and what’s personal?”
claim_review_spans.R8: You don’t need to identify who used it before setting that boundary. A labeled shelf or designated shared-food area could help.
claim_review_spans.R9: > “When I said ‘yeah maybe,’ I meant I wasn’t sure, not that I’d agreed. I realize that wasn’t clear. I’m comfortable discussing visitors, but I’d like us to agree on notice, how often people come over, and keeping the kitchen available for everyone.”
claim_review_spans.R10: You don’t have to choose between accepting every visit and banning guests. You can ask for specific limits that make the home comfortable for you too.
claim_review_spans.R11: > “Let me think about it—I haven’t said yes yet. I’ll let you know by tonight.”
claim_review_spans.R12: And “make yourself at home” can be sincere without explaining the household rules. It’s reasonable to respond, **“Thanks—I’m still figuring out how we share things here. What’s communal, and what should we ask before using?”** Being clear is not the same as being rude. Their response to a clear, reasonable request will tell you more than guessing what they meant.

claim_review_spans.R1: Getting a 48 after spending nearly all week on the paper sounds painful—especially when you’re used to good marks and are still adjusting to studying in English. It makes sense that starting another paper now feels intimidating. I won’t add a load of questions.
claim_review_spans.R2: **You’re not wrong to consider dropping the class. But I don’t think this one mark establishes that dropping is your only sensible option—or that you can’t succeed at university in English.** The feedback points to a specific academic-writing skill, not a verdict on your ability.
claim_review_spans.R3: “Your own argument” usually means **your answer to a question, supported by reasons and evidence**. Changing a reading’s words is paraphrasing: the wording may be yours, but the idea still comes from the source and needs a citation. An argument adds what *you conclude* and explains how the readings support—or challenge—that conclusion. For example:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Although the reading argues X, I think Y is more convincing because Z. The example of ___ supports this because ___.”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t have to invent a completely new theory.
claim_review_spans.R6: 1. **Check only the assignment’s identity.** Look at the course name/code at the top of the page and its assignment title. Compare those with the course’s assignment list. Don’t try to solve the whole paper yet.
claim_review_spans.R7: 2. **If it is due tomorrow—or you still can’t tell—send this now:**
claim_review_spans.R8: > Hi Professor [Name], I had understood that the next paper was due in two weeks, but I’m seeing an assignment page saying tomorrow at 5 p.m. Could you confirm the deadline for [assignment] in [course]? I also realize from my first paper’s feedback that I misunderstood the difference between paraphrasing and developing my own argument. I haven’t started the next paper. If tomorrow is correct, would a short extension be possible? I understand it may not be available. Thank you.
claim_review_spans.R9: 3. **Keep dropping as an option, rather than treating it as decided.** Before submitting a drop, check the deadline and consequences with an academic adviser; if it would change your enrollment load, also check with the international student office. Academic, financial, and immigration implications depend on your circumstances.
claim_review_spans.R10: For the next ten minutes, your task is only to identify that assignment—not to prove you belong at university.

claim_review_spans.R1: I wouldn’t write off the club yet—but I can understand why going back feels uncomfortable. You arrived knowing nobody, took the risk of asking two people to lunch, and got two “busy” replies. Then you stood beside a conversation about plans without knowing whether you were included. That can feel lonely, especially when “give it time” comes from people who already have company.
claim_review_spans.R2: **The hurt is real; the conclusion that they don’t want you around isn’t established.** Two declined lunches tell you those invitations didn’t work out, not necessarily why. Someone sending you memes is at least choosing to keep some contact with you—it doesn’t prove friendship, but it isn’t nothing either. And the Saturday conversation was genuinely ambiguous: it might have been private plans or something open to club members.
claim_review_spans.R3: You don’t have to keep putting yourself through repeated invitations to prove you’re trying. A smaller next step could give you clearer information:
claim_review_spans.R4: - **Read the club chat once, just for information.** You don’t have to reply or look for signs that anyone noticed your absence.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **If there’s an activity you actually like, try one more gathering as an experiment**, not a test of whether people like you. Stay for the activity and aim for one short conversation.
claim_review_spans.R6: - If plans come up again, you can ask: **“Is that a club event, or something you’re organizing separately?”** That’s a normal clarification, not asking people to accept you.
claim_review_spans.R7: With the classmate who sends memes, you could simply respond to one and let that connection develop without another lunch invitation right now.
claim_review_spans.R8: **Showing interest isn’t the same as being desperate.** You can make a small opening and then look for reciprocity: do they ask you questions, continue conversations, suggest another time, or include you later? If repeated visits bring little response or you don’t enjoy the club itself, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. You don’t owe this particular group endless effort.
claim_review_spans.R9: Before these awkward moments, was there anything about the club’s activity that you enjoyed or wanted to explore?
