claim_review_spans.R1: It makes sense that this feels embarrassing, especially when you’re still settling into a new country. But this is a specific payment problem—not evidence that you’re bad with money. You’ve already protected money for food and transport, and you’re checking your options before taking any shifts.
claim_review_spans.R2: - The payment is **800**, and you have **500**, so the shortfall is **300**, not 200.
claim_review_spans.R3: - If today is Monday and payment is due this coming Friday, you have **four days**, not ten. Check the message for the exact calendar date.
claim_review_spans.R4: Being allowed to pay late last time doesn’t automatically mean you have permission again. Asking now gives you time to respond if they say no.
claim_review_spans.R5: > Hi [Name], I received your message about the 800 room payment due this Friday, [date]. I have 500 available toward it and am working on the remaining 300. Would you be willing to accept 500 by Friday and agree on a later date for the balance? Please let me know what date would be acceptable and whether there would be any late fee. I want to confirm an arrangement rather than assume the previous extension applies again.
claim_review_spans.R6: Only agree to a repayment date you reasonably expect to meet, and keep their written response. Check your housing agreement for payment and late-fee terms.
claim_review_spans.R7: - **If it feels safe to speak with your mum**, give her the actual room cost rather than only asking for more:
claim_review_spans.R8: > “I haven’t explained my room cost clearly—it’s 800 per payment. After keeping money for food and transport, I have 500 available, so I’m short 300 this time. Could you help with any of that? I also want us to discuss what’s affordable going forward.”
claim_review_spans.R9: - **Ask your university’s international student office or student support office** where to request emergency housing assistance. Availability, eligibility, and timing vary; I can’t confirm your university’s options. Say:
claim_review_spans.R10: > “I have a 300 housing-payment shortfall due this Friday. Is there emergency assistance I’m eligible for, or someone who can help me negotiate a payment arrangement?”
claim_review_spans.R11: **Being paid in cash does not remove work-authorization requirements.** Whether you can take that job depends on your immigration status and the work involved. You haven’t started, so there’s still time to verify before creating a separate problem.
claim_review_spans.R12: What visa or immigration category are you in, if you know? Just the category—not any document numbers. Meanwhile, the payment-arrangement message is the most useful first move today.

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day can be exhausting, especially only a few weeks after arriving. Getting stuck while explaining a lab result—and then hearing laughter—sounds hurtful. You don’t have to make yourself invisible so nobody has to wait for you.
claim_review_spans.R2: - You heard laughter, but you don’t yet know what they were laughing about. It makes sense that it felt directed at your accent; that isn’t confirmed.
claim_review_spans.R3: - Your name is beside the slides, but that alone doesn’t establish that the group thinks you cannot speak.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Understanding the lab steps when reading alone suggests that explaining under pressure is a particular difficulty—not proof that you don’t understand the work.
claim_review_spans.R5: **My recommendation is to check the grading requirements and request a small, defined speaking part, rather than silently accepting a non-speaking role.** You can decide after that whether it feels manageable.
claim_review_spans.R6: Look for the presentation instructions in your course site, especially “individual contribution,” “oral delivery,” and “group grade.” Neither teammate’s account is confirmed yet. If the instructions are unclear, send the instructor or TA:

claim_review_spans.R1: It sounds uncomfortable to feel you have to stay upstairs—and go hungry—to avoid tension in your own home. Wanting access to the kitchen and a say over your food doesn’t make you difficult.
claim_review_spans.R2: There may be a mismatch in how you and your housemates communicate, but there isn’t enough evidence to conclude that people here don’t care about others’ belongings. They may have heard “yeah maybe” as permission, and “I haven’t eaten” as a request for food rather than concern about missing groceries. Their takeaway offer could have been sincere without addressing what you actually meant.
claim_review_spans.R3: **For right now, you don’t have to resolve the disagreement before eating.** If you feel safe going downstairs, you can simply say:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Hey, I’m going to make myself something to eat. Could I get some space at the counter?”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t have to socialize or explain why you’ve been upstairs. If someone offers takeaway, you’re free to accept or decline; accepting wouldn’t mean agreeing that your groceries are shared.
claim_review_spans.R6: > “I think I haven’t been clear about a couple of things. When I said ‘yeah maybe’ about visitors, I meant I wasn’t sure, not a definite yes. I’d like us to agree on how often we have guests and when we give each other a heads-up. I also noticed some food I bought has been used. I don’t know who used it, but I was keeping it for my meals. Please ask before taking my groceries. Could we work out which food is shared and which is personal?”
claim_review_spans.R7: That explains the misunderstanding without taking blame for someone else using your food. You can acknowledge that you weren’t explicit **and still set a boundary now**.
claim_review_spans.R8: > “Let me think about it—I haven’t said yes yet. I’ll let you know this afternoon.”
claim_review_spans.R9: > “Tonight doesn’t work for me. Could we choose another evening?”
claim_review_spans.R10: “Make yourself at home” is usually a welcome, not a precise agreement about food or visitors. Asking for those agreements isn’t rude; it helps everyone know what to expect. If your housemates keep using your food or dismiss your access to shared spaces **after you’ve clearly raised it**, that’s a different problem from an initial misunderstanding.
claim_review_spans.R11: Does going into the kitchen feel mainly awkward, or are you worried about how someone there might react?

claim_review_spans.R1: Getting a 48 after spending nearly all week on the paper sounds deeply discouraging—especially when you’re used to good marks and are still adjusting to studying in English. Now even the deadline feels uncertain. I won’t give you another list of questions.
claim_review_spans.R2: **You’re not wrong to consider dropping the class. But this mark alone doesn’t show that you can’t succeed at university in English, or that dropping is your only sensible option.** It’s worth keeping that option open without making the decision while you’re this overwhelmed.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Paraphrasing** means expressing a reading’s ideas in different words. That is writing you’ve done, but the ideas still belong to the source and generally need a citation.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **Your own argument** means making a claim that answers the assignment question, then using readings as evidence and explaining how they support—or challenge—your claim.
claim_review_spans.R5: For example: “Author A argues that online classes increase access” summarizes a source. “Online classes improve access only when students also have reliable internet” could be your argument, if it answers the prompt and you support it. You don’t have to invent a completely new idea.
claim_review_spans.R6: 1. **Check which course owns the assignment page.** Look at the course title or code at the top, then the assignment title. Don’t try to write until you know what is actually due.
claim_review_spans.R7: 2. **If it is tomorrow’s paper, send a short message now:**
claim_review_spans.R8: > Dear Professor [Name],
claim_review_spans.R9: > I’ve realized I may have confused the deadlines for two courses. The assignment page for [assignment] says tomorrow at 5 p.m., and I have not started. Would a short extension be possible? I also misunderstood the distinction between paraphrasing the readings and developing my own argument, and would appreciate clarification so I can address the feedback on my first paper. I understand an extension may not be possible.
claim_review_spans.R10: Until an extension is confirmed, treat the posted deadline as active.
claim_review_spans.R11: You don’t have to decide about dropping tonight **unless a withdrawal deadline requires it**. Before actually dropping, check that deadline and any enrollment or immigration consequences with your academic adviser and international student office. That’s not a commitment to stay—it protects your ability to make an informed choice.

claim_review_spans.R1: I wouldn’t write off the club yet—but I understand why going back feels exposing. You arrived knowing nobody, took the risk of inviting two people, and then stood beside a conversation where you couldn’t tell whether you were included. “Making friends takes time” doesn’t do much for the loneliness you’re feeling **now**.
claim_review_spans.R2: The hurt is real; the conclusion that they “obviously don’t want me around” is less certain:
claim_review_spans.R3: - Two people said they were busy on two different days. Those invitations didn’t work out, but you don’t yet know why.
claim_review_spans.R4: - The classmate sending memes is making some contact. That doesn’t prove a close friendship, but it also isn’t something you have to dismiss as mere politeness.
claim_review_spans.R5: - The Saturday conversation was ambiguous. You weren’t clearly invited, but you also couldn’t tell whether it was a club activity or private plans.
claim_review_spans.R6: **My suggestion is one small, low-pressure test—not endless chasing.** Open the club chat just to check for the next activity. If there’s something you’re interested in, consider going with the goal of one brief conversation, rather than getting an invitation or making a friend that day. You could ask:
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I heard people mentioning Saturday last time—was that a club activity or separate plans?”
claim_review_spans.R8: That asks for information without asking anyone to include you in private plans.
claim_review_spans.R9: Inviting someone to lunch isn’t desperate. You can show interest while also noticing whether people eventually reciprocate. If repeated visits bring little welcome or mutual effort, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. You don’t have to keep trying indefinitely—but these few uncertain encounters aren’t enough to establish that you’re unwanted.

claim_review_spans.R1: You’re dealing with a short deadline while still settling into a new country. Asking for help **before taking any shifts or missing the payment** is a sensible step—not evidence that you’re bad with money.
claim_review_spans.R2: - **The shortfall is $300:** $800 due minus $500 available.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **If today is Monday and they mean this Friday, you have four days, not ten.** Check the exact calendar date in the message so you don’t plan around the wrong deadline.
claim_review_spans.R4: Being allowed to pay late last time doesn’t automatically mean you have permission this time. Keep your food and bus money protected, and ask before the deadline:
claim_review_spans.R5: > Hi [name], I received your message that the $800 room payment is due this Friday. I have $500 available for the payment and am working on the remaining $300. Would you agree to $500 by Friday and an extension for the balance? What date could you accept, and would there be any late fee? Please confirm any arrangement in writing. Thank you.
claim_review_spans.R6: Don’t promise a balance-payment date until you have a realistic source for it. Also check any written rental agreement for payment dates and late fees.
claim_review_spans.R7: If it feels safe to discuss money with your mum, give her the actual numbers rather than hiding the room cost:
claim_review_spans.R8: > Mum, I haven’t clearly explained that my room costs $800 per payment. After keeping enough for food and transport, I have $500 toward this Friday’s payment, leaving $300. Are you able to help with any of that? I understand if not; I’m also asking about a payment arrangement.
claim_review_spans.R9: Contact your university’s student support or international student office today:
claim_review_spans.R10: > I’m a new international undergraduate with a $300 housing-payment shortfall due Friday. Are there emergency grants, short-term assistance, or housing support that I’m eligible for? How soon could help be available?
claim_review_spans.R11: Availability, eligibility, and processing time vary; don’t count on funding until confirmed.
claim_review_spans.R12: **Cash payment does not remove work-authorization requirements.** Whether you can take that job depends on your immigration status and the work involved—not your classmate’s assurance. You haven’t started, so you still have time to check with your university’s designated international student adviser or a qualified immigration professional.
claim_review_spans.R13: For now, the smallest useful action is to **confirm Friday’s date and send the payment-arrangement message today**. You don’t have to solve your whole financial situation at once.

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day is tiring, and then getting stuck in front of your group—with laughter you couldn’t explain—sounds hurtful. Being assigned slides afterward could understandably feel like another sign that they don’t want you to speak. But **struggling to explain something in that moment does not establish that you can’t present or that “the quiet one” is your place.** You understand the lab steps when you read them; explaining them aloud under pressure is a different task.
claim_review_spans.R2: There are also some important uncertainties: you don’t yet know what the laughter meant, why the roles were assigned that way, or how speaking is graded. You don’t have to dismiss your discomfort, but you also don’t have to treat your worst interpretation as a settled fact.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **Check the grading requirements before spending more time repeating those three sentences.** Look for the presentation rubric or assignment instructions. If you can’t find them, send the instructor or teaching assistant:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “I’m checking our presentation requirements. Is the grade entirely shared, or is individual speaking assessed separately? Does every group member need to speak?”
claim_review_spans.R5: Your teammates’ conflicting accounts aren’t enough to decide this.
claim_review_spans.R6: 2. **Ask for a small, specific speaking role if you want one.** Preparing slides and speaking need not be mutually exclusive:
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I saw that I’m assigned to prepare the slides. I’d also like to explain our different result during the presentation. Can we reserve a short section for me and do one rehearsal together?”
claim_review_spans.R8: That gives the group a clear request rather than requiring you to prove your overall English ability. If you’d prefer not to speak, check the requirements first so that choice is informed—not driven only by embarrassment.
claim_review_spans.R9: 3. **Practise communicating the point, not producing a flawless paragraph.** Try three short prompts instead of memorizing three exact sentences:
claim_review_spans.R10: Only include an explanation supported by your work; uncertainty is okay. Practise once while looking at the slide, allow pauses, then take a break. You can also use: “Let me say that another way.”
claim_review_spans.R11: If the laughter happens again, a calm response is: “I missed what was funny—was something unclear in my explanation?” You don’t have to confront it now to request participation.
claim_review_spans.R12: **How soon is the presentation?** If you find the grading section, paste just that excerpt with personal details removed, and we can work out what it actually requires.

claim_review_spans.R1: It sounds uncomfortable to feel unsure whether you can use your own kitchen—especially when you’re hungry and still settling into a new country. Wanting your food left alone and some agreement about visitors doesn’t make you difficult.
claim_review_spans.R2: There may be a mismatch in how you and your housemates communicate, but there isn’t enough information to conclude that people here don’t care about others’ belongings. Your “yeah maybe” may have sounded like permission, and “I haven’t eaten yet” may have sounded like a request for food rather than concern about yours being used. Their takeaway offer could have been meant kindly without addressing what was upsetting you. **You can clarify now; you haven’t missed your chance.**
claim_review_spans.R3: **For right now, focus on getting something to eat—not resolving everything.** You don’t need to wait until the visitors leave. If it helps, use one short line:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Hey, I’m just going to make myself something to eat.”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t owe anyone a longer conversation. If going downstairs feels too awkward, you could first message a housemate:
claim_review_spans.R6: > “Hey, I haven’t eaten, so I’m coming down to use the kitchen. Could you leave me some space to cook?”
claim_review_spans.R7: **Later, speak with your housemates without the visitors there.** You can be friendly and clear at the same time:
claim_review_spans.R8: > “I think I wasn’t clear earlier. When I said ‘yeah maybe’ about having friends over, I meant I wasn’t sure—not a definite yes. I’m still getting used to living together, and I’d like us to agree on how often guests come over and how we keep the kitchen usable for everyone.”
claim_review_spans.R9: Then address the food separately, without accusing someone you can’t identify:
claim_review_spans.R10: > “Some food I bought for myself has been used. I hadn’t explained that I was keeping it for my own meals. Going forward, please ask before using my food. Could we agree on what’s shared and what’s individual—maybe separate shelves or labels?”
claim_review_spans.R11: You don’t have to justify the boundary by saying it is normal in your home country. It is a reasonable household preference in its own right. Likewise, “make yourself at home” is usually a welcome, not a precise agreement about food or visitors; those details still need discussing.
claim_review_spans.R12: > “Let me think about it—I haven’t agreed yet. I’ll let you know by this evening.”
claim_review_spans.R13: You don’t have to become blunt or abandon politeness. The goal is to make your meaning easier to understand. If your housemates keep using your food after you’ve clearly asked them not to, that would be a different issue—not just an unspoken misunderstanding.

claim_review_spans.R1: Spending nearly a week on a paper and getting a 48—especially when you were used to good marks—can really shake your confidence. Now the possible deadline is making it harder to write at all.
claim_review_spans.R2: **You’re not wrong to consider dropping the class. But I wouldn’t confirm that it’s your only sensible option, or that this mark means you can’t do university in English.** This feedback points to a particular academic skill you may not have been taught in the same way before—not a verdict on your ability. I won’t give you another load of questions.
claim_review_spans.R3: “Your own argument” usually means **your answer to the assignment question, supported by evidence and your explanation**. Changing the readings’ words is paraphrasing; the ideas still belong to those authors and usually need citations. Paraphrasing can support your argument, but it doesn’t replace it.
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Author A argues X. However, Y suggests that this explanation overlooks Z. Therefore, I argue…”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t need a completely new discovery—just a clear position and reasons for it.
claim_review_spans.R6: 1. **Check only the deadline’s identity.** Look at the course name or code at the top of the assignment page, then the assignment title. If unclear, enter this class through its main course page and open its assignments from there. You don’t need to start writing while you check.
claim_review_spans.R7: 2. **If it is due tomorrow—or you still can’t tell—send this:**
claim_review_spans.R8: > Dear Professor [Name],
claim_review_spans.R9: > I’m seeing an assignment deadline of tomorrow at 5 p.m., but I had understood the next paper was due in two weeks. Could you confirm the deadline for [assignment]? I haven’t started drafting yet. I’m also struggling to understand how to develop my own argument after the feedback on my first paper. If the deadline is tomorrow, would a short extension be possible? I understand it may not be available.
claim_review_spans.R10: 3. **Before submitting a drop request, check the consequences.** An academic adviser can clarify academic and financial effects; your international student office can confirm whether dropping would affect your required enrollment or immigration status. Those rules depend on your situation.
claim_review_spans.R11: Dropping may ultimately be a reasonable choice. You deserve to make that choice with the deadline and consequences clear—not because one painful mark has convinced you that you don’t belong.

claim_review_spans.R1: I wouldn’t write off the club yet—but I can understand why going back feels risky. You arrived knowing nobody, took the initiative twice, and neither invitation led to lunch. Then you were beside a conversation about plans without knowing whether you were included. That can feel especially lonely when everyone else seems settled. “Making friends takes time” doesn’t do much for the hurt right now.
claim_review_spans.R2: At the same time, **these experiences don’t establish that people don’t want you around.** Two people saying they were busy tells you those invitations didn’t work—not necessarily why. The classmate sending memes is at least keeping some contact; it could be casual friendliness rather than just politeness. And the Saturday conversation was genuinely unclear. You didn’t have enough information to know whether it was a private plan or something you could join.
claim_review_spans.R3: Stepping back can protect you from another uncomfortable moment, but leaving every message unread also means missing possible openings. You don’t have to choose between chasing people and disappearing.
claim_review_spans.R4: **My suggestion is one small, low-pressure test before deciding about the club:** read the group chat just to check for the next open event. Reading doesn’t commit you to attending or replying. If there’s an event you find interesting, consider going once more with a smaller goal: take part in the activity and have one brief conversation—not “make a friend tonight.” If plans come up ambiguously again, you can say:
claim_review_spans.R5: > “Is that a club activity, or something you’re organizing separately?”
claim_review_spans.R6: That asks for information without asking anyone to include you in private plans.
claim_review_spans.R7: You can also respond naturally to the next meme without making another lunch invitation. Over time, look for reciprocity: do they ask you things, continue conversations, or suggest another time when they’re unavailable? **You’re allowed to want friendship, and making an invitation isn’t being desperate.** You’re also allowed to redirect your effort if people repeatedly don’t meet you halfway.
claim_review_spans.R8: Apart from this awkward gathering, did you enjoy the club’s activity itself? That matters in deciding whether another visit is worth your energy.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes sense to feel embarrassed, especially while you’re still settling into a new country. But you’ve already protected money for food and transport and checked what you have available. This is a payment shortfall to solve—not proof that you’re bad with money.
claim_review_spans.R2: - The payment is **$800**, and you have **$500** available, so the gap is **$300**, not $200.
claim_review_spans.R3: - If today is Monday and they mean **this coming Friday**, you have about **four days**, not ten. Check the exact calendar date in their message.
claim_review_spans.R4: > Hi [name], I received your message about the $800 room payment due Friday. I have $500 available, but I’m currently $300 short. Would you agree to accept $500 by Friday and arrange a later date for the remaining $300? I’m checking my options today and don’t want to promise a date I can’t meet. Please also confirm the exact due date and whether any late fee would apply. Thank you.
claim_review_spans.R5: Check your rental agreement for payment and late-fee terms, and keep their response in writing. A previous extension doesn’t necessarily authorize another one.
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Your mum, if asking feels safe and realistic:**
claim_review_spans.R7: > Mum, I haven’t explained my room costs clearly. The payment is $800, and after keeping money for food and transport, I have $500 toward it. It’s due Friday. Could you help with the remaining $300 this month? If not, please tell me so I can arrange another option.
claim_review_spans.R8: - **Your university’s student support or international student office:**
claim_review_spans.R9: > I’m an international undergraduate facing a $300 housing-payment shortfall due this Friday. Are there emergency grants, short-term loans, or housing-support options I’m eligible for? What is the earliest assistance could be available?
claim_review_spans.R10: Availability, eligibility, and processing times vary; I can’t confirm your school’s options.
claim_review_spans.R11: **Cash payment does not remove work-authorization requirements.** Whether you can take that job depends on your immigration status and the job itself. Since you haven’t started, check with your university’s international student adviser first. You can ask what authorization, if any, your status requires for that specific job. Don’t count those wages toward Friday’s payment yet.
claim_review_spans.R12: **What exact calendar date does the payment message give?**

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day while adjusting to a new university can be exhausting. Having people laugh when you’re already struggling to explain something can feel humiliating—even when you don’t know what they were laughing about. You shouldn’t have to make yourself invisible so nobody has to wait for you.
claim_review_spans.R2: A few things are still uncertain: the laughter doesn’t establish that your accent was the joke, and being assigned slides doesn’t necessarily mean the group has decided you cannot speak. **Your difficulty getting words out in that moment is not the same as not understanding the lab.** Being able to follow the written steps is important evidence of that distinction.
claim_review_spans.R3: Because the presentation is soon, I’d prioritize these two things over more repetitive practice:
claim_review_spans.R4: **1. Check what is actually being graded.**
claim_review_spans.R5: Look for the presentation instructions or rubric—the criteria used to award marks—on your course page. Neither teammate’s account is confirmed yet. If you can’t find it, send the instructor or teaching assistant:
claim_review_spans.R6: > “Could you clarify whether the presentation has an individual speaking grade, a shared group grade, or both? Is every member expected to speak?”
claim_review_spans.R7: You can paste the relevant grading passage here, with names and personal details removed, and I can help interpret it.
claim_review_spans.R8: **2. Ask for a small, defined speaking part, if you want one.**
claim_review_spans.R9: You don’t have to choose between a long section and complete silence. You could message your group:
claim_review_spans.R10: > “I saw I’m assigned to prepare the slides. I’d also like to present the slide explaining my result and why it differed. Can we confirm speaking roles and do one short rehearsal together?”
claim_review_spans.R11: > “My result was ___. It differed from ___ in ___. One possible explanation is ___.”
claim_review_spans.R12: Practise communicating those points, not reproducing exact wording. During a rehearsal, you can also say: “Give me a moment to finish, please,” or “Which part should I clarify—the result or the explanation?”
claim_review_spans.R13: Preparing slides is a real contribution, and choosing that role can be valid. But it should be a choice informed by the grading requirements and your preferences—not a conclusion that being quiet is your “place.” **How soon is the presentation?**

claim_review_spans.R2: There may be a mismatch between what you meant and what your housemates understood. Their takeaway offer could have been an attempt to include you. That doesn’t make using your food okay; it means you don’t yet know whether this is misunderstanding, an assumed sharing arrangement, or disregard for your things. It isn’t enough to conclude that people here generally don’t care.
claim_review_spans.R3: **For right now, you don’t need to resolve everything before eating.** If you feel safe but awkward going downstairs, you can keep it brief:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “Hey, I’m just going to make myself something to eat.”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t owe the visitors a conversation. If going down feels too uncomfortable, text a housemate:
claim_review_spans.R6: > “Hey, I haven’t eaten and I’m feeling a bit awkward coming down with everyone there. I’m going to come make some food—could you keep some kitchen space clear?”
claim_review_spans.R7: **Later, talk with your housemates when visitors aren’t there.** You can read this from your phone or send it in the house chat:
claim_review_spans.R8: > “I think I wasn’t clear earlier. When I said ‘yeah maybe’ about visitors, I meant I wasn’t sure—not a definite yes. I’d like us to agree on how we handle guests, especially when the kitchen gets busy.
claim_review_spans.R9: > Also, some food I bought for myself has been used. I don’t know who used it, but I was relying on it for meals. Please ask before using my groceries. Could we decide which things are shared and which are personal?”
claim_review_spans.R10: You don’t have to accuse anyone or prove who used the food to set that boundary. A labeled shelf or container can help make the agreement clear, but it isn’t your fault for not having labeled things already.
claim_review_spans.R11: For future invitations, you can be polite without giving an uncertain yes:
claim_review_spans.R12: > “Let me think about it—I’ll get back to you.”
claim_review_spans.R13: > “Tonight doesn’t work for me. Could we do another night?”
claim_review_spans.R14: “Make yourself at home” may be sincere while still leaving everyday rules unspoken. You’re allowed to ask what those rules are—and help shape them. If they keep using your food or dismiss your requests **after you’ve been clear**, that becomes a different issue from an initial misunderstanding.

claim_review_spans.R1: Spending nearly a week on a paper and then seeing 48—especially when you’re used to good marks—can really shake your confidence. Now the possible deadline is making it harder to write anything. I won’t add a load of questions.
claim_review_spans.R2: **You’re not wrong to consider dropping the class. But this mark doesn’t establish that you can’t do university in English, or that dropping is your only sensible option.** It’s worth separating that decision from the immediate shock and deadline confusion.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Making your own argument means giving your answer to the assignment’s question**, then using readings as evidence and explaining how they support—or challenge—your answer. It doesn’t mean inventing something nobody has ever thought before.
claim_review_spans.R4: For example, “Author A says group work improves learning” summarizes a reading. “Group work improves learning only when responsibilities are clear” is a claim you could defend using readings. Without seeing your paper, I can’t tell exactly what the instructor wanted, but “needs your own argument” doesn’t necessarily mean your English was the problem.
claim_review_spans.R5: **For now, do just one thing: identify which class owns the “tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page.** Look at the course name or code at the top, then open the assignment through that course’s main page rather than an old tab. You don’t need to write a sentence yet.
claim_review_spans.R6: > Hello [Name], I’m checking the deadline for [assignment title]. I had understood it was due [date], but the page I’m viewing says tomorrow at 5 p.m. Could you confirm the deadline? I also want to understand how to develop my own argument after the feedback on my first paper.
claim_review_spans.R7: Dropping can remain an option. Before submitting a withdrawal, confirm the deadline and possible effects on your course load, fees, and immigration status with the appropriate university offices; those depend on your circumstances. **You don’t have to prove you belong by staying—but you also don’t have to let one painful mark decide that you don’t.**

claim_review_spans.R1: I wouldn’t write off the club yet—but I understand why going back feels exposing. You arrived knowing nobody, took the risk of asking two people to lunch, and both said they were busy. Then you were beside a conversation about plans without knowing whether you were included. That’s painful, especially when “friendships take time” comes from people who already have company.
claim_review_spans.R2: **What happened is real; what it means is still uncertain.** Two declined invitations don’t establish that people don’t want you around. They might have been busy, or not interested in lunch—we can’t tell yet. The classmate sending memes is at least keeping some contact going; it doesn’t prove a close friendship, but it needn’t be dismissed as mere politeness either. And the Saturday conversation was genuinely unclear, not a definite rejection.
claim_review_spans.R3: You don’t have to keep making invitations while you feel worn down. But there’s a middle option between chasing people and disappearing: **give the club one more low-pressure visit, as a chance to gather information—not a test of whether you’re likable.**
claim_review_spans.R4: - Read only the latest group-chat messages to find the next activity. You don’t need to catch up on everything or post anything.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Choose something you’d enjoy even if you only have one short conversation. Aim to stay through that activity rather than waiting to see whether someone notices you.
claim_review_spans.R6: - If plans come up again, try: **“I missed the context—is that a club activity or something you’ve arranged separately?”** That asks for clarity without assuming an invitation.
claim_review_spans.R7: You can also simply respond to the next meme if it genuinely amuses you. That’s a small, mutual interaction—not another request for someone’s time.
claim_review_spans.R8: **Showing interest isn’t the same as being desperate.** You’ve made two ordinary invitations, not pressured anyone. If, over a few encounters, people repeatedly don’t engage or make room for you, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. But you don’t yet have enough evidence to conclude that you’re unwanted.
claim_review_spans.R9: Apart from feeling left out, was there anything about the club itself that you liked?

claim_review_spans.R1: You’re dealing with a short deadline while still settling into a new country. Feeling embarrassed doesn’t mean you’re bad with money—and asking before taking those shifts gives you time to check the risks.
claim_review_spans.R2: - The payment is **$800**, and you have **$500** available after food and bus costs. That leaves **$300**, not $200.
claim_review_spans.R3: - If today is Monday and payment is due this coming Friday, you have **four days**, not ten. Check the exact date in the message.
claim_review_spans.R4: For now, plan around a **$300 shortfall due Friday**, unless the message says otherwise.
claim_review_spans.R5: Last time’s flexibility is encouraging, but it isn’t permission to pay late again. You could send:
claim_review_spans.R6: > Hi [name], I received your message about the $800 room payment due Friday. I can pay $500 by then, but I’m currently $300 short. Would you agree to accept $500 on Friday and allow an extension for the remaining $300? I’m checking funding options now and don’t yet have a confirmed date for the balance. Could you let me know whether an arrangement is possible, whether any late fee would apply, and confirm the exact due date? Thank you.
claim_review_spans.R7: Only promise a balance-payment date once you know you can meet it. Keep any agreement in writing.
claim_review_spans.R8: - **Your mum, if it feels safe to ask:** Give her the actual cost rather than continuing to hide it:
claim_review_spans.R9: > Mum, I haven’t been clear about my room cost: it’s $800 per payment. After keeping enough for food and transport, I have $500, so I’m $300 short for Friday. Is there any amount you could help with? I understand if you can’t; I’m also asking about an extension and university support.
claim_review_spans.R10: - **Your university:** Ask student support/student affairs or the international student office:
claim_review_spans.R11: > I have a $300 housing-payment shortfall due this Friday. Are there emergency grants, short-term loans, or housing-support options available to international undergraduates? What documents are needed, and could help arrive before Friday?
claim_review_spans.R12: Availability, eligibility, and timing need confirmation; don’t count on funding until approved.
claim_review_spans.R13: **Being paid in cash does not remove work-authorization requirements.** Your classmate’s advice isn’t a reliable basis for starting. Rules depend on your immigration status and the particular job; check with your international student adviser before doing any work, including a trial shift.
claim_review_spans.R14: The first manageable action is sending the payment-arrangement message today. You don’t need to solve your entire budget before asking for more time.

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day while you’re still settling in is exhausting, and that lab interaction sounds hurtful. Getting stuck while explaining a result does **not** mean you have nothing useful to say—or that being quiet is your place in the group.
claim_review_spans.R2: A few important things are still uncertain: what they were laughing at, why you were assigned slides, and whether speaking affects your individual grade. Your feeling that they mocked your accent deserves to be taken seriously, but their intentions aren’t yet clear. Likewise, a slide assignment isn’t proof they’ve decided you cannot speak.
claim_review_spans.R3: **1. Check what is actually assessed.**
claim_review_spans.R4: Look for the presentation instructions or rubric—the criteria used to assign marks. Check for “individual contribution,” “oral delivery,” and whether every member must speak. If you cannot find it, send the instructor or teaching assistant:
claim_review_spans.R5: > “Could you clarify whether the presentation is graded only as a group or whether speaking is assessed individually? Is every group member expected to speak?”
claim_review_spans.R6: You shouldn’t have to rely on conflicting guesses from teammates.
claim_review_spans.R7: **2. Ask for a small, specific speaking role if you want one.**
claim_review_spans.R8: My recommendation is not to give up speaking solely because of this incident. You could write:
claim_review_spans.R9: > “I saw that I’m assigned to prepare the slides. I’d also like to explain our differing result briefly, since I worked on it. Can we include that in the speaking plan and do a short rehearsal?”
claim_review_spans.R10: That asks for participation without requiring you to defend your English. If they refuse, especially if speaking is assessed individually, ask the instructor for help clarifying roles.
claim_review_spans.R11: **3. Make practice easier, not longer.**
claim_review_spans.R12: > “Our result differed from ___.”
claim_review_spans.R13: > “One possible reason is ___.”
claim_review_spans.R14: > “We would need ___ to check that.”
claim_review_spans.R15: Practise one idea at a time, with pauses. If you get stuck, “Let me say that another way” is a perfectly useful presentation phrase. The goal is understandable science, not an accent-free performance.
claim_review_spans.R16: How soon is the presentation? If you find the grading paragraph, paste just that excerpt with personal details removed, and we can work out what it actually requires.

claim_review_spans.R1: Getting a 48 after spending nearly all week on the paper sounds painful—especially when you’re used to good marks and are still adjusting to studying in English. Now the possible deadline is making it harder to write anything. I won’t give you another load of questions.
claim_review_spans.R2: **You’re not wrong to consider dropping the class. But this mark alone doesn’t establish that dropping is your only sensible option—or that you can’t do university in English.** It points to something specific to understand, not a verdict on your ability.
claim_review_spans.R3: “Needs your own argument” usually means something different from “use your own words”:
claim_review_spans.R4: - **Your argument:** making a claim that answers the assignment question, then explaining how evidence from the readings supports it—or where you disagree.
claim_review_spans.R5: For example, instead of only “The author says online learning increases access,” an argument might be: “Online learning increases access only when students also have reliable internet and a suitable place to study.” You don’t need a completely original discovery; you need a position you explain and support. Changing words alone may not meet that expectation, but that is something you can learn.
claim_review_spans.R6: 1. **Check only the course name/code and assignment title** on the page saying “tomorrow at 5 p.m.” Compare them with your course list. You don’t need to start writing yet.
claim_review_spans.R7: 2. **If it is this paper—or you still can’t tell—send this:**
claim_review_spans.R8: > Hi Professor [Name], I’m trying to confirm the deadline for [assignment]. I had understood it was due in two weeks, but I’m seeing a page that says tomorrow at 5 p.m. Could you confirm? I also realize from my first-paper feedback that I misunderstood the difference between paraphrasing and developing my own argument. If tomorrow is correct, would a short extension be possible? I haven’t started the draft yet. Thank you.
claim_review_spans.R9: **Keep dropping as an option, not a conclusion you have to reach tonight.** Before submitting a drop, check the deadline and consequences with academic advising and, if your immigration status has enrollment requirements, the international student office. Those rules depend on your situation.
claim_review_spans.R10: You’re allowed to feel shaken without treating that feeling as proof that you don’t belong here.

claim_review_spans.R1: I wouldn’t conclude that there’s no point going back—but I understand why you’re reluctant. You arrived knowing nobody, took the risk of inviting two people, and got two “busy” replies. Then you were beside a conversation about plans without knowing whether you were included. That can feel especially lonely when everyone else seems already settled.
claim_review_spans.R2: **What happened hurt; what it means is still uncertain.** Two declined invitations don’t establish that people don’t want you around. They could have been busy, or not interested in lunch—we don’t yet know. The classmate sending memes is at least choosing to keep some contact; it isn’t proof of friendship, but it shouldn’t automatically count as rejection either. And the Saturday conversation was genuinely ambiguous, not a clear invitation or a clear exclusion.
claim_review_spans.R3: You’re right that “friendships take time” can sound hollow from people who already have company. You need some sign of connection, not just instructions to keep waiting.
claim_review_spans.R4: Rather than deciding whether to give up on the club altogether, consider **one more visit as a small test**, not a commitment to keep chasing people:
claim_review_spans.R5: - Read just the latest group-chat messages for an upcoming activity. You don’t have to reply or catch up on everything.
claim_review_spans.R6: - At the gathering, aim for one conversation rather than waiting for the whole group to include you. You could say: **“I’m still getting to know people here. How did you get involved in this club?”**
claim_review_spans.R7: - If plans come up again, ask: **“Is that a club activity anyone can join, or something you’ve arranged separately?”** That’s a normal clarification, not an invitation demand.
claim_review_spans.R8: Then notice whether anyone makes room for you—answers warmly, asks you something back, or helps you join an activity. If people repeatedly dismiss you or make no effort in return, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. You don’t have to earn a place by endlessly pursuing them.
claim_review_spans.R9: Taking a break is allowed, too. But asking someone to lunch or checking whether an event is open **isn’t desperate**. You’ve made a couple of reasonable attempts at connection during a very new, uncertain few weeks; those attempts haven’t yet told you where you belong.
